docs.title: chora
docs.text:
chora is the space where forms appear.

chora is a Wayland compositor without policy. It is a programmable scene, not a desktop.

chora has no window manager, no layout, no keybindings and no look. The core renders a small scene of primitives and offers one API. Plugins add all other behavior. A plugin can supply a stacking desktop, a tiling workflow, or a view that an agent arranges live by voice. Only a small safety layer is built in.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Pre-release. chora runs nested inside another Wayland session and as a login session, and a reference plugin tiles the windows. An agent sees and changes the screen through choractl mcp, after a grant of the user. chora is no daily driver yet. The roadmap leads to 1.0: a daily driver with a stable API. The API changes without notice before 1.0.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Each release has an RPM for Fedora 44 and a package for Arch Linux, with SHA256 sums:

sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
sudo dnf install ./chora-*.rpm          # Fedora
sudo pacman -U ./chora-*.pkg.tar.zst    # Arch Linux

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Start chora with the tiling plugin inside a Wayland session:

chora -- chora-tiling

A window opens. The plugin follows the default keymap of the awesome window manager:

Binding Action Super+Return start a terminal (foot) Super+r start a launcher (fuzzel) Super+Shift+c close the focused window Super+j, Super+k focus the next or previous window Super+1 to Super+9 show a tag Super+Shift+1 to Super+Shift+9 move the focused window to a tag Super+space switch to the next layout

chora-tiling --print-config prints all options and bindings. Copy the output to ~/.config/chora/chora-tiling.yaml and change it there. GNOME keeps Super for itself; there, set modifier: Alt in that file.

Nested, chora takes the keymap of the host session. XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT sets another layout, for example XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT=de chora -- chora-tiling. The log names the layouts at the start.

The safety layer has fixed bindings: Ctrl+Alt+Escape resets the scene, Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace quits chora, and Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12 switch the VT.

To let an agent drive chora, grant it screenshots, input and program starts, and add choractl --name agent mcp as an MCP server of the agent:

choractl grant agent screen.capture input.inject activation.token

The agent can then put its own shaders and images, reserve a panel at the edge of the output, wait for clicks and keys, and move the camera. With choractl run it starts programs outside the core, and choractl restart restarts the systemd unit of a plugin (D42).

To try the XP flavor, a stacking desktop in the style of Windows XP, start chora -- chora-xp. From a source tree, put the binaries on PATH, since the plugins start apps with choractl run, and point it at the theme: PATH=$PWD/target/debug:$PATH chora -- chora-xp --theme flavors/xp/theme. Windows wobble while you drag them and minimize through a magic lamp. Ctrl+Alt+Left and Ctrl+Alt+Right, or the desktop buttons 1 to 4 in the taskbar, turn a cube of four desktops. Inside GNOME, which keeps Ctrl+Alt+arrows and Super for itself, use the desktop buttons and the start menu.

To log in to chora on real hardware, choose the session "chora" on the login screen. It starts the tiling flavor with waybar and X11 support through xwayland-satellite. The session "chora (Windows XP)" starts the XP flavor.

Programs inside chora find its IPC socket in CHORA_SOCKET. For example, a terminal in chora shows the scene with choractl query, and choractl events prints the events.

Under examples/ live programs that drive the scene through that socket: the loader prototype (examples/loader) flies a construct of views, HUDs and shaders through the camera, and examples/showcase collects six small apps: snake, pong, two text renderers, a shader card UI and a slide deck.

Agent tools exist today only as external MCP servers on top of existing compositors, for example kwin-mcp, and hypruse for Hyprland. The check found no compositor with an MCP interface of its own. The combination of chora appears to be new: a policy-free core, a scene of primitives with shaders, and one API for plugins and agents.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Build on Smithay and copy from others. Sources: the anvil and smallvil examples, niri, cosmic-comp, Pinnacle. This option gives full control of the scene and the plugin model. This is the decision (D15).
  2. Fork Pinnacle. A working Smithay compositor with an external API on day one. The code review below rejects this option.
  3. River 0.4 with a Rust window manager. No compositor code, but no shaders, no effects and no scene. This option drops the game-engine half of the idea. It is a fallback for a quick tiling prototype.
  4. An MCP server on an existing compositor, like kwin-mcp. This is the fastest way to try agentic workflows. It gives no canvas and no effects.

River shows a strong design for the window manager interface. chora can copy its semantics without its code.

docs.title: Pinnacle code review
docs.text:
The review measured a clone of Pinnacle 0.2.2 (last commit 2026-06-27).

  • Size: 34,138 lines of Rust in src/. The workspace adds the client API (Rust and Lua), the Snowcap widget toolkit and a wlcs test adapter.
  • Policy in the core: tags touch 20 files, layout modes 20 files, window rules 8 files. Click-to-focus is hardcoded.
  • Rendering: a flat list of Smithay render elements on top of Smithay's Space. No scene graph and no custom shaders. Space appears in 23 files.
  • API: tonic gRPC with 115 methods around tags and layout modes. No batching and no transactions for clients.
  • Transactions: yes, for window positions per output. A transaction completes when every window commits, or after 150 ms. The design comes from niri.
  • License: GPL-3.0-or-later. src/protocol/drm.rs is GPL-3.0-only. The API crates and Snowcap are MPL-2.0.
  • Activity: 57 commits in February 2026, then 2, 3 and 8 per month.

A fork keeps about 40 to 50 percent of src/. It deletes or rewrites the spine that chora replaces: Space, the window state, tags and the API. Only the generic parts survive, and these are easy to copy. Dependencies lists them.

docs.title: Plugin runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Strengths Weaknesses Extism on wasmtime more than 13 guest languages, simple, sandboxed bytes in, bytes out: every call serializes and copies wasmtime with the Component Model typed WIT interfaces, handles to scene nodes, fuel and epoch limits, fast new instances fewer mature guest languages; Rust is first-class wasmer works less momentum for the Component Model mlua with LuaJIT or Luau low friction, easy reload, Luau sandbox no memory isolation from the host Rhai pure Rust, easy slow tree-walking interpreter Rune native to Rust not at 1.0 deno_core (V8) JS and TS ecosystem heavy, GC pauses, API churn abi_stable dylibs native speed stale, unsafe unloading, no sandbox IPC clients (separate processes) any language, crash isolation from the OS, no runtime in the core a round trip per event; no code in every frame

For code in every frame, the Component Model is better than Extism. Typed calls only help when the boundary stays typed: JSON over WIT gives back the cost of Extism. chora starts with IPC clients only (D28). wasmtime comes when a measurement demands it.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
• niri, cosmic-comp and Pinnacle use the GLES renderer of Smithay. Custom GLSL shaders through texture and pixel shader elements work in practice, for example the blur of niri.
  • No Smithay compositor renders through wgpu. The Smithay maintainers consider wgpu too abstract for a compositor. Smithay has no merged Vulkan renderer either.
  • Decision: a scene renderer of chora on GLES 3, with GLSL (D17).

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: rmcp 3.x supports stdio and Streamable HTTP. choractl mcp uses stdio. A container gets the socket through a bind mount, so chora needs no network transport.

docs.title: Widgets and shells
docs.text:
Quickshell is the strongest choice: Qt6 and QML, declarative, with live reload. waybar is mature. eww and AGS/Astal need a check of their activity. All of these need wlr-layer-shell.

For HTML from agents, a browser in app mode (chromium --app=...) is enough (D38). chora places toplevels anywhere. A dedicated host on gtk4-layer-shell with WebKitGTK, or a Tauri window as a layer surface, is an option for later.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Before 1.0

The API changes without notice before 1.0 (D3). The Roadmap lists the planned changes. Plugins, choractl and agents use one language of commands and events.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A command changes the scene. An event reports a change. Commands travel in transactions (see Architecture). Ownership decides who may change a node.

# one transaction
- create: {id: work, kind: group, parent: root}
- create: {id: bar, kind: rect, parent: work, props: {size: [1280, 30], color: [0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1]}}
- attach: {surface: s42, parent: work}
- configure: {surface: s42, size: [900, 600], states: [activated]}
- update: {id: s42, props: {transform: {translate: [40, 40]}}}
- focus: {surface: s42}

create and update take the node properties in props. Unknown fields are errors, so a typo never passes silently.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
The nodes form a tree under root, which the cameras show. Each output has a second root, screen:NAME, for example screen:DP-1 (D43). Its nodes stay fixed to the screen: they sit in the logical coordinates of the output, without its camera, above the scene and below the top and overlay layers of layer shell. A HUD or a progress bar goes there, also during an animated camera move. The nodes under screen:NAME work as all others, with input, effects and ownership. The overlay root stays when its output goes, with its nodes, for the return of the output; the emergency reset empties it.

This table is the one list of node properties.

Property Nodes Meaning id all stable id; ids of the form s1, s2 belong to surfaces, and the core assigns them; chora:inject belongs to the injection mark of the core owner all client name of the owner; read-only focused all true in scene.query on the surface with the keyboard focus and on the node of focus_node; read-only, left out on all other nodes rects all in scene.query: the output name maps to [x, y, w, h] in logical pixels of that output. The core applies all parent transforms and the camera, and projects like the renderer. The query leaves out outputs where the node does not show. The box holds the drawn shape under rotation, perspective or a mesh. A clip or an ancestor layer cuts the box to its own box. The mesh of a layer does not move the boxes of its descendants. Read-only. to surface the only client name that can attach this detached surface, after a remove with to or for a new toplevel; read-only claim all [x, y, w, h] in scene coordinates: the area of the owner as a window manager; a new toplevel can go to it (see below); null removes the claim transform all a 4x4 matrix in column-major order, with the translation at the indices 12 to 14, or the short form translate, scale, rotate opacity, visible all clip group, rect, image, shader {"radius": r}: the node and its descendants show only inside its size, with corners rounded by r logical pixels, and take pointer input only there; the node becomes a layer; null removes the clip effects group, rect, image up to 8 effects {"shader": path, "uniforms": {name: number or 2 to 4 numbers}}; the node becomes a layer, and the core applies the shaders in order; an image without a size has the size of its file; for a group, the area of its layer mesh group, rect, image cols and rows from 1 to 64, and points: the place of each grid point in node coordinates, row by row from the top left; optional depth: the z of each point, which the transform of the node projects; the node becomes a layer that shows through the grid; points: [] removes the mesh color rect, text RGBA, each from 0 to 1, with straight alpha: [1, 1, 1, 0.5] is white at half opacity radius rect the radius of the corners in logical pixels; the rect becomes a layer border rect {"width": w, "color": [r, g, b, a]}: a line of w logical pixels along the inner edge; the rect becomes a layer; null removes it image image absolute path of a PNG file; the core loads it again after a change slice image insets left, top, right, bottom in pixels of the file: the corners keep their size, the edges and the center stretch shader, uniforms shader the absolute path of a GLSL ES fragment shader, and its uniforms as for an effect; a uniform {"node": id} is a sampler2D with that node as it shows on its own, at most 4 text, family, font_size, max_width text text: UTF-8, needed at create, at most 4 KiB; family: a font family, at most 4 KiB, a system font without it; font_size: logical pixels, from 1 to 1024; max_width: the width at which lines wrap, and nothing else; a text node has no size, it sizes itself by its layout, so it is never a layer: rotated, mirrored or projected outside a layer, it draws nothing, so put it in a group with a size and a clip; the core draws it in color, white at 16 logical pixels by default; the raster limit is 16 MiB per output scale, and 256 MiB for all text nodes together; a raster beyond the second limit draws nothing until its node changes; a text beyond it at scale 1 gets no rect and no draw; a text beyond it only at another scale draws nothing at that scale

A surface node gets its size from its client. The configure command asks the client for a new size.

A shader node draws its shader over its size, as a layer. Its children render into uniform sampler2D tex, and the shader gets the same inputs as an effect. A node texture shows the node without its transform, at its size or, for a surface, at the size of the window. A node with opacity 0 hides in the scene and still shows in a node texture. Inside a node texture, shader nodes get no node textures of their own, so that two shader nodes that read each other do not recurse.

# a rounded button with a border, a round clip and a shader that reads it
- create: {id: button, kind: rect, parent: root, props: {size: [120, 40], color: [0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1], radius: 8, border: {width: 2, color: [1, 1, 1, 1]}}}
- create: {id: avatar, kind: group, parent: root, props: {size: [64, 64], clip: {radius: 32}}}
- create: {id: glow, kind: shader, parent: root, props: {size: [400, 300], shader: /home/me/glow.frag, uniforms: {strength: 0.5, picture: {node: avatar}}}}
- update: {id: button, props: {border: null}}

A node with a size and a mesh, or with a transform that is not a plain 2D translation and scale, for example a rotation or a perspective, is a layer (see Architecture). animate moves the points of a mesh of the same grid, for example for a magic lamp minimize.

With depth, a grid bends into 3D, for example a strip on a ring around the viewer, and a perspective transform projects it. The texture maps perspective-correct. A triangle with a point behind the viewer does not show; the rest of the mesh does.

An effect is a GLSL ES fragment shader with absolute path. It reads the layer in uniform sampler2D tex at varying vec2 v_uv. v_uv is (0, 0) at the top left of the node and grows to the right and down, as the scene does; a flame that rises therefore rises toward small v_uv.y. A shader node and an effect may use uniform float alpha, uniform vec2 size (the texture size in pixels), uniform float time (seconds) and its own float and vec2 to vec4 uniforms. The texture holds premultiplied colors, and the shader writes premultiplied colors; the core passes the uniforms as they are, so a color uniform is whatever the shader takes it to be. A transaction that names a shader that does not compile fails with the log of the compiler. The core compiles a shader again when its file changes. The package installs examples in /usr/share/chora/shaders/: grayscale.frag, rounded.frag and blur.frag (with radius).

Two hints for shaders. With precision mediump float, the common hash fract(sin(dot(p, …)) * 43758.5) loses its digits and gives garbage; noise and hashes need precision highp float. fwidth, dFdx and dFdy need GL_OES_standard_derivatives, which the core enables for a shader that uses them.

The core loads the file of an image when a transaction names it, on a worker thread: the transaction answers when the file is decoded, while other clients go on, and the later transactions of the same connection wait for it. A file that does not load, that is larger than 32 MiB or larger than 8192 pixels on a side rejects the transaction. A plugin in a container shares its asset directory with the core, as it shares the socket directory.

A client that shares no directory with the core, for example an agent in another container, hands its files to the core with assets.put. The core stores them in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/ and answers with the absolute path for image, shader and effects. A file has at most 512 KiB, a client at most 64 files, all clients together at most 64 MiB. A client name with assets has at most 120 bytes. A second put of a name replaces the file, and the nodes that use it load it again. The files of a client go with its nodes. With keep_nodes, they go when chora exits. With resume only, they go after the grace time. Otherwise, they go at the last disconnect. choractl asset put NAME FILE prints the path.

docs.title: Commands
Keyboard focus of nodes
docs.text:
The chrome of a plugin, for example a menu or a dialog, is made of nodes and takes the keyboard with focus_node:

{"focus_node": {"node": "start-menu"}}

While the node has the focus, no surface gets keys: the focused surface gets a leave, and the core sends each key as node.key to the connections of the owner of the node that subscribed to it. A press carries the text that it types:

{"event": "node.key", "node": "start-menu", "key": "a", "code": 30,
 "state": "pressed", "modifiers": ["Shift"], "text": "A"}
  • key is the keysym name with the modifiers applied, code the Linux key code, and modifiers lists Ctrl, Alt, Shift and Super as they are down.
  • text is missing for a release, for a key without text such as Return, and while Ctrl, Alt or Super is down. A dead key types nothing; the core does no compose.
  • The core repeats a held key as a Wayland client does: after 200 ms, 25 times a second, with the same pressed event. Modifiers do not repeat. The repeat ends when the key goes up, when another key goes down, or when the node loses the focus.
  • The safety layer and the grabs come first, also for injected keys.

The focus returns to the focused surface, which gets an enter, in these cases:

  • The owner sends {"focus_node": {}}.
  • The node goes.
  • Its client disconnects, also with keep_nodes or resume.
  • The session locks.
  • A surface gets the focus, by a command or by the core.

A layer surface that takes the keyboard exclusively, for example a launcher, gets the keys before the node. Some layer surfaces take the keyboard on demand, for example the search field of a panel. A click on such a surface ends the focus of the node and gives it the keyboard.

docs.title: Window managers
docs.text:
Several window managers share the scene (D55). A window manager sets claim on a node, for example on its root group. At the first commit of a toplevel, the core reserves it for one window manager:

  1. the owner of its parent toplevel, for a dialog;
  2. else the owner of the node or surface with the keyboard focus, if it holds a claim;
  3. else the owner of the smallest claim that contains the pointer.

Only clients with a connection or in their grace time count. Only the chosen client can attach the surface, and surface.created names it in to. Without a match, any client attaches the surface. When the last connection of the client closes, the reservation ends with surface.detached. With resume, it ends at the end of the grace time. When a window manager removes its last claim, its reservations end too. A remove with to hands a surface to another window manager in the same way.

docs.title: Selectors
docs.text:
A selector finds nodes: id:work, kind:surface, owner:tiling, app_id:firefox, title:"make test" (exact), title~:Inbox (contains), meta:role=editor. Conditions separated by spaces must all match. A value with spaces goes in double quotes. An empty selector or * matches every node. Selectors work in queries only. A query returns all current matches, or an empty list. It always sees the current titles.

scene.query also takes a JSON filter next to the selector: {"selector": "kind:surface", "filter": {"owner": "tiling", "focused": true}}. The fields are owner, kind, app_id, focused: true, visible: true and output: "NAME". All of them must match, and so must the selector. focused keeps the surface with the keyboard focus and the node of focus_node. visible keeps nodes that show on some output, output nodes that show on that one. Both read the rects of the result, so an invisible node matches neither. An empty filter matches everything; focused and visible filter only when true. Unknown fields fail.

choractl wait SELECTOR polls the query every 100 ms until something matches, then prints the matches as one JSON line and exits 0. --gone waits until nothing matches. --timeout SECS limits the wait, 10 seconds by default; a timeout exits 1 with the reason on stderr.

docs.title: Events
IPC methods
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line, on the socket in CHORA_SOCKET. A client sends hello first. A method that changes the session or needs a grant fails before hello. scene.query, events.subscribe, output.list, clients.list, clients.create, methods.list, camera.release, grants.set, grants.revoke and grants.list also work before it, for tools.

The core opens an admin socket next to the IPC socket, for example wayland-1.admin.sock next to wayland-1.sock (D40). It offers all methods. Only there do grants.set, grants.revoke and clients.create work. choractl grant, choractl revoke and choractl clients create use it; choractl clients up [FILE] applies a YAML file of NAME: { grants: [...] } entries: it opens the socket of every name with exactly the capabilities of the list (D33, D40). A socket with the equal capabilities stays (clients.create answers the socket_exists reason) with its connections; changed capabilities recreate the socket and disconnect its Wayland clients. While a name is connected or in its grace time the socket cannot open (clients.create answers the connected reason); choractl clients up then syncs the grants of that name. It reports both reasons and goes on with the remaining names. Without a file argument the first of $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/clients.yaml and ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml is read, - for stdin. The core answers every request.

Method Purpose hello(name, keep_nodes, resume, protocol, features) name the client (lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., from a letter, at most 64 bytes); keep_nodes keeps its nodes and cameras after the disconnect, resume keeps them for a grace time (see below); protocol and features say what the client speaks (see Protocol versions); returns {"version": ..., "protocol": ..., "features": [...]} scene.query(selector, filter) read nodes scene.apply(commands) apply a transaction events.subscribe(events) stream the named events, or all events for an empty list, as notifications; answers with a snapshot of the scene first (see Events); each subscribed connection gets each event, also when several connections share a client name; an unknown name is refused input.grab(binding) get the events of a key or a pointer button with modifiers, for example Super+Return or Super+BTN_LEFT; a binding needs Ctrl, Alt or Super unless the client has the capability input.grab-any; Ctrl+Alt with a key of the safety layer stays refused either way; returns the binding as input.key and input.button name it input.ungrab(binding) end a grab of this connection; a grab also ends with its connection input.inject(events) send synthetic input: pointer, buttons, scrolling, keys, shortcuts and text; needs a grant screen.capture(output, node, max_side) capture an output or a node as a PNG file; needs a grant camera.release(output) take the camera of an output away from its owner, live or gone, without telling it, so that the view goes back to its default and any client can own the camera again; the old owner takes the camera back with its next camera command; works only on the admin socket, choractl camera release OUTPUT calls it grants.set(client, capabilities), grants.revoke(client, capabilities), grants.list grant or revoke capabilities for a client name. choractl grant and choractl revoke call them. grants.set and grants.revoke work only on the admin socket. A name with a client socket answers code 9, because clients.yaml holds its capabilities. For a name of the main socket, methods.call changes nothing, and activation.token only opens the MCP tool run_program. clients.create(name, capabilities) open the client socket of a name with exactly those capabilities and return its path (see Client sockets); equal capabilities keep the socket and give back what the revoke binding took, changed ones recreate it; without capabilities, an existing socket keeps its own; only on the admin socket; choractl clients create NAME and choractl clients up call it output.list list the outputs and their cameras output.reserve(output, edges) leave space at the edges of an output out of its work area while the connection lives, as the exclusive zone of a panel does; edges has top, right, bottom and left in logical pixels, and no space removes the reserve; returns the output output.configure(output, scale, transform) set the scale or the transform of an output, the first one without output; transform is normal, 90, 180, 270, flipped, flipped-90, flipped-180 or flipped-270; scale and mode must keep the logical size within 16384 pixels a side; returns the output output.add(spec), output.remove(output) for tests on the headless backend only: add a virtual output WxH[@SCALE][+X+Y], which returns the output, or remove one, as a monitor plugs in or out; the mode side has 1 to 16384 pixels and WxH divided by SCALE must stay within 16384 a side and at most 16 outputs are live; other backends refuse, and the last output stays; choractl add-output and choractl remove-output call them clients.list list the connected client names and the methods that each exported methods.export(names) offer methods of this client to other clients methods.list list the methods that clients exported, each with its description and input schema methods.call(client, method, params) call a method of another client; the answer is the result of the method; a client socket needs the capability methods.call methods.return(call, result, error) answer a method.called event activation.token answer an xdg activation token of no client, for choractl run (D42, see Programs); the next toplevel that activates with it shows the token in surface.created; one use ends it; an unused token of no client is forgotten after 10 s; a client socket needs the capability activation.token assets.put(name, data) store a file in base64 for image nodes, shader nodes and effects; returns its path assets.remove(name) remove a file of assets.put

An error has a code, a message and, where it helps, a machine readable data. Error codes lists the stable codes. A rejected transaction carries {"command": INDEX} in data, the position of the failed command in the transaction.

A request is one line of at most 1 MiB (MAX_LINE). The core reads a longer line to its end, answers it with code 6 and the id null, and closes the connection. The core holds at most 8 MiB (MAX_OUTPUT) of answers and events that a connection did not read yet; a connection that passes this limit closes, so a client reads its socket while it waits. An answer that does not fit, for example of a query of all nodes, fails with code 6 instead, and the connection stays.

The core takes at most 128 connections, at most 16 of one process. The last 8 go only to a process without a connection, so choractl and a window manager that starts again still connect while one client holds many. A refused connection gets an error line with code 6 and the reason, too many connections: ..., before the core closes it.

hello answers with the version of the core: the crate version and, for a build in a git checkout, the commit, for example {"version": "0.5.4+1ea0e89abc", "protocol": 1, "features": []}. See "Protocol versions" for the other two fields. chora --version prints the same version. The client library of chora-scene warns once on stderr when the core is another build, so choractl and the plugins tell why a request fails after an update.

A connection sends hello once, within 5 s. Connections with the same name share their nodes, so they must agree on keep_nodes and resume. The core refuses a hello with different values. For example, choractl --name tiling fails while the tiling plugin runs. With keep_nodes, resume has no effect. A hello with resume also fails while another connection of the name is live. So a second instance of a plugin cannot take the nodes of the first. The error says that the name is connected.

resume lets a plugin restart without a loss, for example after a crash or a change of its configuration. When the last connection of a name with resume closes, the core keeps the nodes of the name for a grace time of 10 s. It keeps their tree, stacking, properties and meta. It also keeps the surfaces that they hold, the cameras and the assets. The grabs, the exported methods, the reserves and the keyboard focus of a node end as at any disconnect, and client.disconnected follows at once.

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "hello", "params": {"name": "wm", "resume": true}}
  • A hello of the same name with resume within the grace time gets the nodes back. The plugin finds them with scene.query and owner:NAME. When the list is not empty, it rebuilds its model from them instead of creating its nodes again.
  • A hello of the name without resume removes the kept nodes first, so the client starts as without a grace time.
  • After the grace time, the core removes the nodes as at any disconnect: the surfaces become detached, and the core sends surface.detached for each.
  • No client of another name can change the kept nodes. Only a name with a client socket is safe from other clients that take it (see Client sockets).
  • A toplevel that maps during the grace time gets surface.created as usual, and stays without an owner if no other plugin attaches it. The resumed plugin takes it as at any start, with a query of kind:surface for surfaces without an owner.
  • The emergency reset and a disconnect of the watchdog end the grace time at once.

A reserve of output.reserve belongs to a connection and ends with it, also when its client crashes. The reserves of all connections on an output add up, and count from the edges of the area that the exclusive zones of layer surfaces leave free. At least one pixel of the work area stays. choractl reserve --top 30 holds a reserve until it ends.

A key binding needs Ctrl, Alt or Super, so that typing still works, unless the client holds input.grab-any (D45). The bindings of the safety layer, Ctrl+Alt with BackSpace, Escape, i or F1 to F12, belong to no client. A binding has one owner at a time. Revoking input.grab-any drops the registrations of grabs that need no modifier and ends a held one.

A key grab is held from the press of its key until one of its modifiers Ctrl, Alt or Super goes up; a grab without any of them ends with the release of its own key. Shift does not end a key grab. Each press of the key in that time sends pressed; the release of the key sends nothing and reaches no surface. When the grab ends, the client gets one released. So an Alt+Tab switcher sees Alt down, Tab, Tab, Alt up as pressed, pressed, released, and knows when to switch.

A button binding names a pointer button in place of the key: BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT, BTN_MIDDLE, BTN_SIDE, BTN_EXTRA, BTN_FORWARD or BTN_BACK. It needs Ctrl, Alt or Super too, or input.grab-any, so that a plain click still works. While its button is down, the client of the grab gets the press, each move and the release, also when the modifiers went up first, and no surface gets them:

{"event": "input.button", "binding": "Super+BTN_LEFT", "state": "pressed",
 "position": [812, 140], "output": "DP-1", "local": [812, 140]}
{"event": "input.moved", "binding": "Super+BTN_LEFT",
 "position": [830, 152], "output": "DP-1", "local": [830, 152]}

A window manager moves a window with Super+BTN_LEFT so, wherever the pointer grabs it.

The core implements wlr-output-management, so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs (see Architecture). output.configure sets the scale and the transform on the same path (D44), for an agent without wlr-randr. After a new mode, position, transform or scale, the core sends output.changed. For an output that turns off, it sends output.removed, and output.list no longer lists the output.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
Each failure has a stable code (T2). The negative codes are the JSON-RPC codes for requests the core cannot route. The positive codes name the kind of refusal, and a client can act on them without reading the message.

code kind example -32700 the line is no JSON request a line without a JSON object -32601 no method of this name scene.drop -32602 parameters are missing or invalid scene.query with "selector": 3 1 the request breaks a rule of the scene or of the core updating a node of another client 2 a surface node of a transaction is gone a window closed during the wait 3 a protocol the core does not speak a hello with protocol 2 (D29) 4 a capability the method needs screen.capture without a grant 5 an unknown node update of a node id that never existed 6 a limit of the core is reached a request longer than 1 MiB 7 a client name that is taken a hello with a name that has a client socket 8 a method of the admin socket grants.set on the main socket 9 a rule of client sockets a hello with another name on clients/agent/ipc.sock

Code 1 stays for every refusal the table has no own code for, for example a scene rule. The message always names the rule. A plugin can ignore code 2. A rejected transaction, so codes 1, 2, 5 and 6, carries the index of the failed command in data.

docs.title: Protocol versions
docs.text:
Both sides of the IPC say which protocol they speak (D29). hello takes an optional protocol, an integer, and a list features. It answers with the protocol, the features and the version of the core:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "hello", "params": {"name": "wm", "protocol": 1, "features": []}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": {"version": "0.7.0+1ea0e89", "protocol": 1, "features": []}}

The core speaks protocol 1. It refuses a client with a higher protocol with code 3, and the client must upgrade its core. A lower protocol works, so an older client keeps running. A missing protocol means a client from before the versioning, and works. Compatible additions arrive as named features while the protocol stays 1; a breaking change raises the number. The core answers with its own list, never with a mix. The client library of chora-scene sends its own protocol and features. It warns once on stderr when the core answers with another protocol.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
input.inject and screen.capture see or drive the whole session, and input.grab-any lets a client catch keys and buttons without a modifier, so they need a grant of the user for the client name. A name with a client socket needs no grant: clients.create and clients.yaml give it the capabilities (D33, D40):

$ choractl grant agent screen.capture input.inject
$ choractl grants
{"agent": ["input.inject", "screen.capture"]}
$ choractl revoke agent

A grant lasts until choractl revoke or the end of the session. The emergency reset revokes all grants. A connection through a client socket instead has exactly the capabilities the socket was opened with. A recreate with changed capabilities ends the Wayland clients that connected before it, and so does the reset. Only the admin socket changes grants. A process of the user on the host reaches the admin socket too. So a grant protects against hostile code only when that code sees its client socket alone, with the gaps that Client sockets lists. choractl mcp offers no tool for grants. On the main socket, activation.token opens the MCP tool run_program, and methods.call changes nothing.

docs.title: Client sockets
docs.text:
A client socket fixes the name of its clients (D33). clients.create on the admin socket opens clients/NAME/ipc.sock below the directory of the main socket, which has mode 0700. capabilities says what a connection through it may do; clients.yaml and clients up fill it in. choractl clients create agent prints its path:

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "clients.create", "params": {"name": "agent", "capabilities": ["screen.capture"]}}
  • clients.create also opens clients/NAME/wayland.sock, a Wayland socket for the windows of the client. Its answer has the path of the IPC socket and the wayland path.
  • A connection through it says hello with that name only.
  • It cannot change grants or make client sockets, as these need the admin socket.
  • It fixes the name, confines the files and narrows the scene. On it, scene.apply follows these rules. A refusal by one of them has code 9, names its rule and carries the index of the command in data. The rules of the scene keep codes 1, 2, 5 and 6:
  • focus_node with a node needs the last press of the user on a node or a window of the name. The press counts once, and a key press ends it.
  • A name that holds the focus of a node moves it to its other nodes without a press.
  • No create or move puts a node under screen:* or below it.
  • No camera command works.
  • attach, focus, close and configure take only a window of its own wayland.sock or a surface that the name owns. focus needs a press as focus_node does, also to drop the focus.
  • scene.query on it returns only the nodes of the name and the windows of its wayland.sock. The surface.* events come only for these windows.
  • A claim of the name gets only the new windows of its wayland.sock.
  • The socket has exactly the capabilities of its clients.create; the other methods answer by them. A process that may use the socket drives the session as far as they reach.
  • grants.set and grants.revoke answer code 9 for the name: change clients.yaml and run choractl clients up.
  • methods.call needs the capability methods.call, and activation.token the capability activation.token. Without them both answer code 4. The main socket needs neither. A token of activation.token belongs to no client. Any window that activates with it takes the focus without a press, also a window of the client itself. With methods.call, a client can also ask a window manager for the focus. So both capabilities let a client take the keyboard. A window of its wayland.sock asks for tokens through xdg-activation, under the focus rules above.
  • Its image, shader and effect paths name only its own files of assets.put. The main socket has no such rule: a client of it runs as the same account as the core and could read those files anyway.
  • It holds at most 16 connections, and its Wayland socket at most 16 clients. All client sockets together leave 32 connections to the main socket.
  • The main socket refuses a hello with a name that has a client socket, so no client of the main socket takes that name.
  • Equal capabilities keep an existing socket. clients.create answers the socket_exists reason with the path of that socket. choractl clients create NAME prints NAME has a client socket already: PATH on stderr and exits 1. Changed capabilities recreate the socket at the same path and disconnect its Wayland clients.
  • clients.create fails for a name with a connection or in its grace time, and beyond 64 client sockets.
  • The name has lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., and starts with a letter, at most 64 bytes; hello and clients.create refuse everything else. Its socket path must fit a Unix socket. A second clients.create of a name takes only other capabilities.
  • The emergency reset removes the client sockets, and so does the exit of chora.

The callers of methods.call are certain only for names with a client socket.

A Wayland client of wayland.sock gets the protocols of the main Wayland socket, with these exceptions:

  • Screencopy and image capture need the grant screen.capture of the name.
  • The input method needs the grant input.inject.
  • Output management, the session lock, both foreign toplevel protocols, the security context manager, idle inhibit and idle notify are not offered. On Wayland the client cannot lock the session, list the windows, control the windows of others, open a socket of its own or keep the screen awake. On ipc.sock, focus_node and focus take the keyboard only after a press of the user on the client, as a token below does.

The layer shell stays, so a panel can run in a container. Such a client can draw over all windows in the top layer, but the core refuses the overlay layer. A layer surface of it takes the keyboard on demand at most, never exclusively. After a click on it, it gets the keys until a click goes elsewhere. So a full-screen panel can look like a lock screen and read what the user types into it.

An xdg-activation token or a popup grab of such a client needs the serial of its last key or button press, and never 0. A token also needs the keyboard focus on the client, and uses the press up. So the client takes the focus only after input, once per press. Synthetic input from input.inject sets that serial too, so a client with that grant can create the press itself. When the token is used, it must still be at most 10 s old and the client must still have the keyboard focus.

The client gets the capabilities of the socket at the time it connects. A recreate with changed capabilities disconnects it, and so does the emergency reset. Its frames of screencopy and image capture that wait then get nothing. Its socket closes at its next request. Its windows carry the name: a query shows it in surface.client. It reads the clipboard only while it has the keyboard focus, as every Wayland client does.

A container that mounts only its client directory cannot take another name or give itself capabilities.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
The core starts no program except its own startup command (D30, D42). choractl run starts programs outside the core, and systemd keeps plugins running.

choractl run [--] CMD ARGS... starts a program outside the core. It asks the core for an activation token with activation.token and passes it to the program in XDG_ACTIVATION_TOKEN. It prints the pid, the unit and the token as one JSON line while the program runs.

  • When systemctl --user is-system-running shows a state other than offline, a user manager runs. systemd-run --user then starts the program in the transient unit chora-run-PID-TIME.service. journalctl --user -u UNIT shows its output. The unit lives until the last process in it ends, so an app that a launcher starts lives on. The arguments reach the program literally, without the expansion of $ by systemd.
  • This needs systemd 254 or later. When systemd-run fails, for example because the unit exists already, run exits 1 with its error and starts nothing.
  • The unit gets the environment of the user manager, plus the token. PATH, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET get the value of the caller, or none when the caller has none. It gets DISPLAY and the other host session variables only from the caller, never from the user manager. It starts in the directory of the caller.
  • Without a running user manager, choractl starts the program itself, with the environment of the caller. The program stays in the process group of the caller. Its output goes to /dev/null, and unit is null.
  • When the unit starts but its MainPID stays unknown after a short wait, for example because the program ended at once, pid is null. The command never starts the program twice.

A window that activates with the token before its first commit, or in the same batch, shows the token in surface.created. chora-tiling and chora-xp start apps with choractl run too, so a restart of a window manager leaves its apps running.

$ choractl run -- foot
{"pid":4343,"token":"a1b2c3d4e5f60718","unit":"chora-run-4342-1761400000123456789.service"}

choractl restart NAME restarts a plugin with systemctl --user restart. The unit is chora-NAME-SESSION.service of a view in this session, where SESSION is a short hash of CHORA_SOCKET. Else it is chora-NAME.service of a flavor (see Plugins). The flavor unit counts only in the session whose WAYLAND_DISPLAY the user manager holds, so a nested chora never restarts a plugin of its host. A name without an active unit is an error: the command exits 1 with the reason on stderr, and starts nothing. It prints the unit as one JSON line and calls no core.

$ choractl restart tiling
{"unit":"chora-tiling.service"}

docs.title: Screen capture
docs.text:
screen.capture renders an output, or a node with its descendants, and answers with a PNG file in base64:

Parameter Meaning output the output name; the first output if neither output nor node is set node a node id, for example a surface or a group max_side shrink the picture until its longer side has at most this many pixels

The result has the width and height in pixels, the scale in pixels per logical pixel, the origin and the png. A pixel at (px, py) shows the point origin + (px, py) / scale: in the logical coordinates of the output, whose origin is (0, 0), or in the coordinates of the node.

  • An output shows as on screen, without the cursor.
  • A node shows without its own transform, opacity, mesh and effects, on a transparent background, but with its rounded corners, border, clip and the shader of a shader node. Its area covers the descendants with a size.
  • A picture has at most 16 Mi pixels and 8192 pixels a side; a larger one shrinks. max_side must be at least 1.
  • A capture renders the scene again. Layers that the pixel budget of the last frame left out of the screen show in the capture; left_out names them, and layers.dropped tells it as it happens.
  • A capture fails while the session is locked, and when the PNG file is larger than 5 MiB; a smaller max_side helps then.

choractl capture FILE saves a picture, for example choractl --name agent capture --node s1 window.png.

docs.title: Input injection
docs.text:
input.inject sends a list of events as one request:

{"events": [
  {"pointer_move": {"position": [640, 400], "output": "DP-1"}},
  {"click": {"button": 272}},
  {"text": {"text": "make test\n"}},
  {"shortcut": {"keys": "Super+Return"}}
]}

A click on a node needs no client math, whatever pan, zoom or parent scale the scene shows:

{"events": [
  {"pointer_move": {"node": "menu", "point": [10, 20]}},
  {"click": {"button": 272}}
]}
Event Fields pointer_move position in the logical coordinates of the output, as in a capture; output, the first one by default; or node with point inside it button button, a Linux code, 272 (left) by default; state: pressed or released; hold: a press stays down when the request ends click button; presses and releases it scroll dx and dy in logical pixels; a positive dy scrolls down key key: a keysym name such as Return, or a Linux key code such as 28; state shortcut keys, a binding such as Ctrl+Shift+t: the modifiers go down, the key goes down and up, the modifiers go up text text; with an enabled text input at the focus the core commits the whole string, else a newline presses Return, a tab presses Tab
  • node and point replace position. The core maps the point through the same transforms that give the rects of a query for the node. The point must lie in the box the node draws. An output limits the search to that output, and a node that shows no such point rejects the request.
  • The core checks all events before the first one runs. An event that does not resolve, for example a character without a key, rejects the request.
  • Without an enabled text input at the focus, key names and text use the first layout of the keymap. A character then needs a key with Shift or AltGr at most.
  • A focused surface with an enabled text input receives each text whole as one commit. The commit carries characters the keymap cannot reach, for example German umlauts on a US layout.
  • Keys and buttons that the events leave down go up at the end of the request, so that no key sticks.
  • A button press with hold stays down. A later button event releases it, in the same request or in a later one.
  • Injected keys never reach the safety layer: Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace, Ctrl+Alt+Escape, Ctrl+Alt+i and the VT switch do nothing. The grabs of plugins see them, and the focused surface gets the rest.
  • Every executed request shows the injection mark: a small yellow rect of the core next to the pointer, gone 500 ms after the last injected event (see Safety layer).
  • A request has at most 256 events, 4096 characters of text in all and 32,768 steps, a key press and a release being two. It fails while the session is locked.
  • With "dry_run": true next to events, the core checks every event and answers ok or the error, without sending input.

choractl inject reads the list of events as JSON, for example echo '[{"text": {"text": "ls\n"}}]' | choractl --name agent inject. choractl inject --dry-run checks the events without sending input.

docs.title: Plugin methods
docs.text:
A plugin exports methods, and other clients call them by the client name and the method name, for example tiling.set_layout:

$ choractl call tiling set_layout '{"layout": "fair"}'
{"columns": 1, "gap": 4, "layout": "fair", "master_width": 0.5, "masters": 1, "windows": ["s2", "s1"]}

The core sends the exporting connection a method.called event. The plugin answers with methods.return: the same call and a result, or an error with a code and a message. The core passes the answer to the caller. The Client of chora-scene answers with Client::answer.

Each entry of methods.export is a plain name, or an object with name, description and input_schema. methods.list answers every exported method as {"client", "name", "description", "input_schema"}, with null for a plain export. The core passes description and schema through unchanged, and chora-tiling gives one to each of its methods.

  • A method name has at most 64 characters: lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., starting with a letter.
  • A connection exports at most 64 methods. Another connection of the same client name cannot export the same method.
  • A call without an answer fails after 10 s, and so does a call whose exporter disconnects. A connection has at most 64 calls in flight, and it cannot call its own methods.

chora-tiling exports these three; chora-tiling lists all of its methods:

Method Parameters Result set_layout layout of the current tag: tile, tile_left, tile_bottom, tile_top, fair, fair_horizontal, spiral, dwindle, max, fullscreen, magnifier or floating; gap in logical pixels; a missing field keeps its value the layout, the gap, master_width, masters and columns of the current tag, and the windows that show on the current output get_layout none the same give to: a client name hands the focused window to to with a remove with to, and answers with its surface id

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin is a client with a manifest:

name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
configure: set_layout

choractl view load reads the manifest of each plugin of a view: it starts a plugin that does not run with exec, and passes the config of the view to the method in configure (see Configuration). The start goes through choractl run. With a user manager, the unit chora-NAME-SESSION.service restarts the plugin when it fails. It carries the session, so that every chora on the same user manager starts its own plugins. A flavor starts its plugins as its own systemd units chora-NAME.service instead. A view whose plugin unit runs already, for example while the plugin starts, waits for that plugin. choractl view load works only from the main socket: a view connects as view-NAME, and a client socket refuses any name but its own.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
choractl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio (D34). It connects as the client agent, or under --name. An MCP client starts it, for example in the .mcp.json of Claude Code:

{"mcpServers": {"chora": {"command": "choractl", "args": ["--name", "agent", "mcp"]}}}
Tool Purpose describe_screen a screenshot of an output, at most 1280 pixels a side by default, and in words: the outputs, the windows with their positions in scene coordinates and sizes, and the plugins with their methods capture a picture of an output or of a node, as screen.capture, at most 1920 pixels a side by default query_scene the nodes of a selector apply_commands a transaction list_plugins the connected clients and their methods call_method a method of a plugin, for example tiling.set_layout inject_input synthetic input, as input.inject load_view, save_view, unload_view the views of Configuration, by name only run_program start a program as choractl run does, on the machine of the MCP server; answers pid, unit and token, or the error of the start; the output of the program never comes back reserve_space space at the edges of an output, as output.reserve, while the server runs configure_output the scale or the transform of an output, as output.configure put_asset a file for image nodes, shader nodes and effects, as assets.put: name, and text for a shader or base64 for a PNG; returns the path subscribe_events start to collect events, and grab keys and buttons; events and keys as in events.subscribe and input.grab; replaces the current subscription wait_events the collected events: waits up to timeout_ms (5000 by default, at most 30000) for the first one, and returns at most max (50 by default, at most 500, 0 takes nothing)

The input schemas of apply_commands and inject_input come from the types of chora-scene. They list every command, every input event and every field, with its description, so the model sees the shape of a call before the first try. A test checks that the schemas, the types and the examples of this page agree.

The screenshot of describe_screen, capture and inject_input need the grants of the client name, for example choractl grant agent screen.capture. Without a grant, describe_screen still describes the scene. No tool grants anything (D40). On a client socket, call_method and the tools of plugin methods need the capability methods.call. run_program needs the grant activation.token on every socket, because a started program can do all that the user can. On the main socket, choractl grant agent activation.token gives it; a client socket lists it in clients.yaml. The program starts where the MCP server runs, for example inside the container of an agent.

A subscription has a connection of its own under the same client name. A thread reads its events into a buffer of 1000 events, so the core never waits for the agent. When the buffer is full, the oldest events go, and wait_events counts them in dropped. The grabs of the keys end with the subscription.

A tool that fails, also on invalid arguments, answers with isError and the reason, so that the model can correct its call. An unknown tool is a JSON-RPC error.

Every method that a plugin exports is a tool of its own, named client.method, with the description and the input schema of the export. call_method stays for the general case. The tool list answers fresh on every tools/list, so a later methods.export needs no restart. A call of such a tool passes its whole arguments object as the params of the method.

While the core is not reachable, tools/list answers with the built-in tools alone and logs the reason on stderr. The plugin tools come back with the next call.

The server answers requests in parallel: a running wait_events blocks no other call. A notifications/cancelled ends the wait of wait_events within 100 ms; the cancelled call gets no answer, as the protocol keeps it.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Current state

This page describes the implementation. The Roadmap lists the planned changes, and the Decisions give the reasons.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["chora (Rust, Smithay)"]
        protocols["Wayland protocols"]
        backends["Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput, winit for development, headless for tests"]
        scene["Scene: group, surface, rect, image, shader, text"]
        render["Renderer: GLES and GLSL shaders"]
        input["Input router"]
        ipc["IPC socket: JSON-RPC"]
        safety["Safety layer"]
    end
    clients["Wayland clients: apps, Quickshell, waybar, browsers"] <--> protocols
    plugins["Plugins: WM, layouts, keybindings"] <--> ipc
    choractl["choractl: CLI and MCP bridge"] <--> ipc
    services["Services in containers"] <--> ipc
    agents["Agents: MCP clients"] <--> choractl
    services -.-> clients
    plugins -.-> clients

The core has one language: commands and events (see API). Plugins, choractl, services and agents all use it. Nothing outside the core changes the scene in another way.

Plugins are separate processes (D28). A plugin can also be a Wayland client, for example to draw window decorations as its own surfaces.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The compositor binary chora. Its tasks, and nothing more:

  • Wayland protocol handling and the client lifecycle, through Smithay.
  • Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput on real hardware, through libseat. A winit window for development inside another compositor. chora uses winit when WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY is set, and the hardware otherwise. On hardware it draws the cursor of the xcursor theme in XCURSOR_THEME. chora --headless 1280x800 runs on virtual outputs for tests and agents: the software renderer of Mesa draws each output into a texture at 60 Hz, with damage, and input comes only from input.inject. It needs no host display, GPU or seat.
  • The scene. The core renders it for each output.
  • Input routing (see below).
  • The IPC socket.
  • The safety layer (see below).
  • The startup command: chora -- <command> runs one command with WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET set. The command does not get the variables that reach a host compositor, for example WAYLAND_SOCKET and SWAYSOCK. Without a command, the core shows a black screen.

The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces itself, because the protocols define their position. Smithay's PopupManager and LayerMap do this work. Layer surfaces, for example panels and launchers, sit in the coordinates of their output, outside its camera, so a panel stays in place when a plugin pans the scene. The background and bottom layers are below the scene, the top and overlay layers above it. A panel reserves an exclusive zone, and an IPC client reserves space with output.reserve; the rest of the output is its work area. Only toplevels wait for a plugin: the core creates a detached surface node and sends surface.created. A plugin decides where the surface appears, or if it appears at all.

Taskbars see the toplevels through ext-foreign-toplevel-list and wlr-foreign-toplevel-management. A handle of the second protocol reports the title, the application id and the outputs that show the surface. Its states are activated for the surface that plugins focused, and maximized and fullscreen from the last configure. The core never reports minimized. The requests of a taskbar, close included, go to plugins as surface.requested.

Screenshot tools and screen sharing capture outputs through wlr-screencopy, for example grim, OBS and xdg-desktop-portal-wlr (D37). A frame offers an shm buffer in XRGB8888. The core renders the output into it as on screen, without the cursor. Frames of both protocols wait for the next tick, one refresh later: each tick renders each output or toplevel once for all its frames, and a client has at most four frames waiting, so that no client can make the core render more than once per refresh and source. Newer tools use ext-image-copy-capture, which also captures a toplevel of ext-foreign-toplevel-list; the toplevel shows as screen.capture shows its node. Frames of both protocols fail while the session is locked. The renderer writes into shm buffers in shm.rs, which is the one place with unsafe code besides the GL calls in gl.rs.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text: The scene is a tree of nodes with stable ids. API lists the node properties. The order of the children sets the stacking order. The crate chora-scene holds the scene model (see Project structure).

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Each client names itself when it connects. The owner of a node is a client name, not a connection, so several choractl calls share their nodes.

  • Only the owner changes or removes a node.
  • A detached surface has no owner. The client that attaches it becomes its owner.
  • A child under a group does not change the group. The child keeps its own owner.
  • The removal of a group removes its descendants. Surfaces among them become detached.
  • When the last connection of a name closes, the core removes the nodes of that name. Its surfaces become detached. A client that connects with keep_nodes, for example choractl, keeps its nodes. A client that connects with resume keeps them for a grace time. A restart within the grace time gets them back (see API).

docs.title: Cameras
docs.text:
All outputs show one logical scene. Each output has a camera: a transform from scene coordinates to the logical coordinates of the output. The output scale then gives the pixels.

  • The default camera follows the output layout of wlr-output-management. An output at position (x, y) shows the scene area from (x, y) with the logical size of the output. Scene and layout coordinates then agree.
  • The camera command replaces the default, for example to pan or zoom. A camera is a 2D translation of at most 10^7 and a scale from 1/64 to 64. It ignores the z axis, so a uniform scale such as {"scale": 1.5} works. A camera needs an output that is plugged in or was, so no client claims an output before it appears. The first client that sets the camera of an output owns it. When the owner disconnects, the output gets its default camera back, unless the owner keeps its nodes with keep_nodes, or with resume until the end of its grace time. The reset restores all default cameras.
  • Two outputs side by side get two adjacent default cameras. A window across two outputs then needs no special case.

docs.title: Output configuration
docs.text: The core implements wlr-output-management (D27), so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs. Every output of the backend is a head of the protocol, also while it is off. A head can get a mode, a position, a transform and a scale, or turn off. The core tests a configuration as a whole before it applies it. If one part fails, the core changes nothing and answers failed. One output must stay on. After a change, the core places the layer surfaces again and announces the outputs to plugins (see API). On winit, the window decides the mode, and the output cannot turn off. Headless outputs accept every change; tests add and remove them with output.add and output.remove, as monitors that plug in and out. No backend has adaptive sync.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
The core uses Smithay's GLES renderer through Smithay's own renderer traits. Custom shaders give blur, rounded corners, shadows, color effects and transitions. niri shows what this approach can do. An effect is a GLSL ES fragment shader that a node names; the node becomes a layer, and each effect is one pass over its texture. The core compiles a shader when a transaction names it, rejects the transaction on an error, and compiles it again when the file changes.

Transforms are 4x4 matrices, so 3D effects need no API change. A node with a size and a mesh, or with a transform that is not a plain 2D translation and scale, is a layer: the core renders it with its descendants into a texture of its size, and then draws the texture through the mesh, or a quad, with the full transform of the node and the camera. The vertices go to the GPU in homogeneous coordinates, so textures map correctly under perspective. Wobbly windows move the points of a mesh, a magic lamp animates them, and a desktop cube turns layers in 3D. A layer has no depth test: the order of the siblings decides what is in front, and a plugin hides the faces that turn away. Pointer input reaches the nodes of a layer only where its transform is a plain 2D one.

The core asks each output for a frame once per refresh. It renders only when the damage tracker of Smithay reports damage. A layer counts as changed in every frame, so a scene with a layer renders in every frame. There is no direct scanout. Milestone 0.10 replaces this with a renderer of chora that renders only on damage (D17, D24).

A text node lays out and draws inside the core. cosmic-text shapes the text with the system fonts and the fonts of every directory in CHORA_FONT_DIRS. It falls back per character, so CJK and emoji show without a font choice. A changed prop lays out the node again; a new output scale rasterizes it again. One cache entry per node holds the layout size and the raster of each physical scale.

The cost of a frame grows with the number of visible nodes: a node is a draw call with its own texture, and software GL spends roughly 60 to 140 µs on one. A headless session at 1280x800 on llvmpipe holds about 250 animated nodes at 60 fps; the renderer of 0.10 moves the ceiling.

docs.title: IPC socket
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line, on a Unix socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora/. The socket has the name of the Wayland display, for example wayland-1.sock. The core exports the path as CHORA_SOCKET. calloop serves the socket in the event loop of the core, so no thread handoff is necessary. Events are JSON-RPC notifications on the same connection.

When a client closes its side of the connection, the core still answers the requests that arrived, also those of waiting transactions and methods.call. Then it closes the connection.

Limits keep a buggy client from exhausting the core:

Limit Value Effect connections 128, 16 per process, the last 8 for processes without one the core sends an error line and closes the new connection time until hello 5 s the core closes the connection line length 1 MiB the core answers with an error and closes the connection output buffer of a connection 8 MiB the core closes the connection; an answer that does not fit becomes an error waiting transactions of a connection 16 the core rejects the transaction nodes other than surfaces 16,384 the core rejects the create cameras 64 the core rejects the camera meta of a node 32 keys, 1 KiB per key or value, 4 KiB in all the core rejects the command

A plugin can export methods, for example tiling.set_layout. The core forwards a method call to the plugin as an event and returns the answer to the caller. A call without an answer fails after 10 s. An agent then asks the window manager for a change instead of fighting it (see API).

docs.title: choractl and the MCP bridge
docs.text: choractl is the CLI for the coordinator. It loads views and starts their plugins. choractl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio, with tools for whole tasks such as describe_screen (see API). MCP stays out of the core, so the MCP side can change without a change to the compositor.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction is a batch of commands. The core applies it as one unit.

Some commands need a client round trip. A resize sends a configure event, and the client must answer with a new buffer. The core therefore holds the transaction until all affected clients commit, or until a deadline of 150 ms passes. Then the core shows all changes in the same frame (D22). Until then, a commit blocker holds each answer, so no new buffer shows early, at the old place.

A surface that misses the deadline is late. No transaction waits for it until it commits a buffer for its newest configure. A hung client thus delays the queue once, not once per transaction.

A transaction that names an image file waits until a worker thread has decoded the file, so a large PNG does not stop the event loop. It waits outside the queue: the transactions of other connections, input and frames go on, and only the later transactions of the same connection wait behind it. A file that fails to decode rejects the transaction.

docs.title: Frame flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Backend
    participant C as Core
    participant R as Renderer
    B->>C: vblank
    C->>C: apply the transactions that are ready
    C->>C: advance the running animations
    C->>R: render the damaged parts of each camera
    R-->>B: page flip

docs.title: Input flow
docs.text:
1. libinput sends an event to the core.
  2. The safety layer checks its fixed bindings first.
  3. The plugins that grabbed the key or the pointer get the event. A plugin consumes the event or lets it pass.
  4. The focused surface gets each event that no plugin consumed. Pointer events go to the topmost node under the cursor that accepts input. The inverse of the camera maps the cursor to scene coordinates.

Plugins set the focus. The core changes it in three cases only:

  • The emergency reset focuses the first surface.
  • A click on a surface without an owner focuses it.
  • A surface that becomes detached, unmaps or goes away loses the focus.

The core still implements the protocol mechanisms around focus: popup grabs, the keyboard interactivity of wlr-layer-shell and ext-session-lock, the locks and confinements of pointer-constraints, and text-input with input-method. Activation requests of xdg-activation and of taskbars go to plugins as surface.requested. A layer surface that takes the keyboard exclusively, for example a launcher, has it from its first commit until it goes away, and it ends a popup grab.

A click gives the keyboard to a layer surface that accepts it on demand, and ends the keyboard focus of a node. The layer surface keeps it until one of these occurs:

  • A click goes elsewhere, or a surface gets the focus.
  • Its role goes, or it no longer accepts the keyboard.
  • Its output goes.

A popup grabs the input only with the serial of the last press, or of the last key or button event that its client got. A release counts, so a menu opens on F10 when the key goes up.

docs.title: Safety layer
docs.text:
The safety layer is the only built-in behavior (see Vision). No plugin and no IPC client can change it.

  • Fixed bindings (D23). Injected input never triggers them; see Input injection. They are Ctrl+Alt+BackSpace (quit), Ctrl+Alt+Escape (emergency reset), Ctrl+Alt+i (revoke) and Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12 (VT switch).
  • Revoke binding. Ctrl+Alt+i takes every capability away from every client and drops the unused activation tokens of no client. It also ends the grabs that need no modifier and disconnects the Wayland clients that a capability gave a protocol, for example screencopy. The IPC connections stay.
  • Injection mark. While a client injects input, the core shows a small yellow rect of its own next to the pointer. It goes 500 ms after the last injected event. No client owns the mark or can remove it.
  • SIGUSR1 starts the emergency reset too, for example from a text console when the keyboard no longer reaches the compositor.
  • Last words. A faulting signal (SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGABRT) writes the fault address and a backtrace to stderr before the default action ends chora. tests/last-words.sh checks it.
  • Emergency reset. The core disconnects all plugins and ends their grace times. It revokes all grants, removes all effects and restores the default cameras. It puts all surfaces in a simple grid. This grid is the one layout in the core. It is hardcoded, so a broken configuration cannot break it. The reset also changes the focus (see Input flow).
  • Session lock. The core enforces ext-session-lock. One client owns the lock; other clients cannot lock or unlock while it lives. While the session is locked, each output shows only its lock surface, or black. Only the lock client gets input; popup and pointer grabs end, and plugin grabs pause; a keyboard grab, for example of an input method, ends before each key. The core confirms the lock after each output showed a frame that it rendered under this lock. When the lock client crashes, the session stays locked, and only then can a new lock client take over.
  • Watchdog. When frames take longer to render than a refresh of their output for two seconds, the core blames the client whose visible nodes cost the most: a node counts 1, a layer and each effect 25 more. It removes the effects, the meshes and the shaders of shader nodes of that client and sends effects.dropped with its name. When frames stay slow for two more seconds, the core disconnects that client, at most once a minute. It does so only when that client's own load reaches the owner budget (D57). CHORA_OWNER_LOAD_BUDGET sets that budget, 4000 by default. The nodes of a disconnected client go as on any disconnect, also those of a client with keep_nodes or resume, without a grace time. When no client alone reaches the budget, the watchdog drops the effects of all clients and disconnects none. The watchdog never starts the emergency reset; only the binding and SIGUSR1 do.
  • Shader hangs. A shader that never returns blocks the loop, for every backend renders on it. Neither the watchdog, which measures between frames, nor SIGUSR1, whose source the loop dispatches, can end it: on llvmpipe the core hangs, on a GPU until the driver resets the context. The way out is to kill the core from another TTY or over SSH.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
chora trusts every client of the same user. One gap comes with the Rust Wayland backend: a message whose size is not a multiple of four leaves that connection deaf instead of answered with a protocol error, and the core has no frame of its own to reject. Correct clients send no such message. The caps of the IPC socket (16 connections per process, 128 in total) and of the client sockets (16) bound the harm; the main Wayland socket has no cap. Client sockets fix the name and the capabilities of a client (D33, D40). The Wayland socket of a client socket offers the privileged protocols only with grants. Only the admin socket of choractl changes grants and makes client sockets (see API).

  • Unsandboxed Wayland clients get all protocols, as in sway. So any client can, for example, take the keyboard as an input method, or configure the outputs.
  • A sandbox such as Flatpak connects its apps through a socket of wp-security-context-v1. Those clients do not see the privileged protocols: the layer shell, the session lock, the input method, both foreign toplevel protocols, output management, both screencopy protocols with their sources, and the security context manager itself.
  • The IPC methods input.inject and screen.capture need a grant of the user for the client name: choractl grant NAME CAPABILITY. A grant protects against mistakes of agents. It is no barrier against hostile code of the same user. The emergency reset revokes all grants.
  • screen.capture and input.inject fail while the session is locked.
  • The core starts no program except its own startup command (D42). choractl run starts programs outside it, and systemd units keep plugins running.
  • A connection of a client socket acts only on its own nodes and on the windows of its wayland.sock. It sets no camera and puts no node under screen:*. It takes the keyboard with focus_node or focus only after a press of the user on it (see API).

docs.title: Sessions and flavors
docs.text:
• The session file chora.desktop runs chora-session tiling. The script imports the environment of the login into the systemd user manager and starts the user service chora@tiling.service. It waits until chora ends, and then stops the units of the graphical session.
  • Without XKB_DEFAULT_LAYOUT, chora-session takes the keyboard layout of the system from localectl.
  • chora@.service runs chora -- chora-flavor <name> as part of graphical-session.target. It drops WAYLAND_DISPLAY and DISPLAY that another session left in the user manager, which would make chora run nested.
  • chora-flavor <name> imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET into the systemd user manager, and DISPLAY when xwayland-satellite is installed. It links the units of the flavor until the next boot, tells systemd that chora is ready, and starts the target of the flavor. Units of the flavor then find the compositor and the IPC socket. The script is not for nested use: the variables would reach the units of the host session.
  • The tiling flavor starts chora-tiling, waybar if it is installed, and xwayland-satellite on a free X11 display for X11 programs (D26).
  • A derived secureblue image installs the package (D10, D14).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Views are YAML files in git, and an agent can read and write them. A strict schema validates each file. It rejects unknown keys and catches the YAML traps, for example no read as false.

The core reads no configuration file. It runs one startup command (D30), for example chora-flavor, which starts the systemd target of a flavor:

chora -- chora-flavor tiling

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
~/.config/chora/
├── views/              # one file per view
├── flavors/            # bundles of views, plugins and services
├── plugins/            # plugin manifests
├── shaders/            # GLSL ES shaders
├── clients.yaml        # the names and capabilities of `clients up`
└── chora-tiling.yaml   # the options and bindings of chora-tiling

The directory is a git repository. It contains no secrets. The package installs the reference flavors to /usr/share/chora/.

Fonts are not there: the core draws text with the system fonts and with every directory listed in CHORA_FONT_DIRS, separated by :. A user font in ~/.local/share/fonts needs no setting at all.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a part of the scene and the plugins that drive it (D35):

# ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml
name: work
plugins:
- name: tiling
  config: {layout: fair, gap: 12}
scene:
- id: work-corner
  kind: group
  props:
    transform: {translate: [1800, 20]}
- id: work-badge
  kind: rect
  parent: work-corner
  props:
    size: [100, 30]
    color: [0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0]
  • choractl view load work starts each plugin of the view that does not run yet, with the exec of its manifest, and waits up to 10 s until it connects. It passes each config to the method that the manifest names in configure. Then it applies the nodes of the view as one transaction.
  • The client view-work owns the nodes. A second load replaces them, choractl view unload work removes them.
  • choractl view save work writes the nodes of view-work as they are now, with the plugins of the file that was there, to ~/.config/chora/views/work.yaml, or to --file PATH. A plugin or an agent changes the nodes as view-work, for example choractl --name view-work apply.
  • A node has an id, a kind (group, rect, image, shader or text), a parent (the root by default) and its props as in a create command.
