  • A name has lowercase letters, digits, _, - and ., and starts with a letter, so that its file stays in its directory. A name does not end in .yaml, because such a name is a path. The file NAME.yaml must name the same view.
  • choractl view load also takes the path of a YAML file; the MCP tools take names only.
  • A plugin that a view starts gets no stdin and no stdout of choractl, which carry MCP under choractl mcp.

choractl looks for NAME.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/chora/views/ first (~/.config/chora/views/ by default), and then in /usr/share/chora/views/.

docs.title: Strict YAML
docs.text: choractl reads views and manifests with serde-saphyr (D41). Unknown keys, duplicate keys and unknown tags are errors. Only true and false are booleans, so no stays the string no.

docs.title: Plugin manifests
docs.text:
A manifest tells choractl how to start and how to configure a plugin. It lives in plugins/NAME.yaml of the same directories:

# /usr/share/chora/plugins/tiling.yaml
name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
configure: set_layout
description: Tiles the windows with the tags and layouts of awesome.
Key Meaning name the client name of the plugin exec the shell command that starts it configure the exported method that takes the config of a view; a view without config needs none description what the plugin does

The package installs the manifest of chora-tiling.

docs.title: Clients file
docs.text:
choractl clients up [FILE] applies a file that maps client names to their grants (see API):

# ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml
agent:
  grants: [screen.capture]
showroom:
  grants: []

The grants are the five capabilities of choractl grant (see API). An agent that drives the window manager needs methods.call, and one that starts apps needs activation.token. Both let it take the keyboard focus.

The names follow the rules of hello. clients up opens the socket of every name with exactly the capabilities of its list. A socket that already has the equal capabilities stays with its connections and gets them back after the revoke binding. Changed capabilities recreate the socket and disconnect its Wayland clients. A name with a client socket takes no choractl grant and no choractl revoke; the file decides. While a name is connected, its socket cannot open. clients up then only syncs the grants of the name and says on stderr that the socket stays closed.

docs.title: chora-tiling
docs.text:
chora-tiling connects with the client name tiling. Grants and choractl restart use this name.

chora-tiling reads chora/chora-tiling.yaml in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by default ~/.config, or the file of --config. Without a file, it uses its default, which chora-tiling --print-config prints. The file lists every option:

Option Meaning modifier what MOD means in the bindings: Super or Alt gap the gap around each window, in logical pixels tags the number of tags of each output, at most 16 layouts the layouts in the order of next_layout; each tag starts with the first master_width, masters, columns the start values of each tag for the tile layouts new_window master or stack: where a new window goes focus click or follow_mouse bindings a binding with MOD, and its action; the default file uses every action at least once; run: CMD starts a shell command with choractl run

The layouts and the default bindings follow the awesome window manager. Each output has its own tags, and each tag its own layout and parameters. A window can be on several tags, and an output can show several tags. A floating, maximized or fullscreen window leaves the tiles. A click or a binding raises the window that it focuses; the focus that follows the pointer raises nothing. The binding MOD+Ctrl+r reads the file again. Mouse moves and resizes of floating windows do not exist.

chora-tiling exports methods for other clients (see Plugin methods). Every method but get_layout changes something and answers with the layout info of the current tag, like set_layout.

Method Parameters Does the same as set_layout, get_layout see API the layout of the current tag give to: a client name handing the focused window to another client view_tag tag: a tag number MOD+1 to MOD+9 move_to_tag surface, tag MOD+Shift+1 to MOD+Shift+9, for this window focus surface a click: focuses and raises the window, and its output; a window that shows nowhere only gets the urgent mark focus_next, focus_prev none MOD+j and MOD+k swap_master surface MOD+Ctrl+Return, for this window

chora-tiling connects with resume (see API). It keeps the tags and the layouts of each output, and the tags, the states and the stacking of each window, in the meta of its nodes. A restart within the grace time rebuilds them from there. In a flavor or a view, choractl restart tiling does that after a rebuild.

chora-tiling claims the box around the work areas of its outputs (D55). --output NAME limits it to some outputs, as for chora-xp, and can come more than once. So each window manager takes its own outputs. It leaves a new window that the core reserves for another client to that client. When the last of its --output outputs goes, it gives its windows away, and another window manager adopts them. It takes new windows again when one of its outputs comes back. Next to chora-xp, tiling needs modifier: Super: with Alt, tiling grabs Alt+Space for next_layout, and the system menu of XP does not open.

docs.title: Flavors
docs.text:
A flavor is a directory with views, plugin manifests and services, plus a systemd user target chora-<name>.target. chora-flavor <name> looks for the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/ first and then in /usr/share/chora/flavors/. It imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY, CHORA_SOCKET and the X11 DISPLAY of xwayland-satellite into the systemd user manager, so that every unit of the flavor starts with them. It links the units of the directory, and starts the target. The target starts the services and the plugins. systemd handles start, restart and order, so chora needs no service manager.

The package installs the tiling flavor:

/usr/share/chora/flavors/tiling/
├── chora-tiling.target              # wants the two units below
├── chora-tiling.service             # chora-tiling
└── chora-tiling-xwayland.service    # xwayland-satellite, if installed

The target also wants waybar.service, which the waybar package installs. A copy of the directory in ~/.config/chora/flavors/tiling/ replaces it.

docs.title: The XP flavor
docs.text:
The XP flavor is the showroom (D39): a stacking desktop in the style of Windows XP. It is a demo, not a daily driver. chora-xp connects with the client name xp.

/usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/
├── chora-xp.target              # wants the two units below
├── chora-xp.service             # chora-xp
├── chora-xp-xwayland.service    # xwayland-satellite, if installed
└── theme/                       # SVG files, fonts, wallpaper and cursors

The session "chora (Windows XP)" on the login screen starts it with the XP cursors, which the package installs to /usr/share/icons/ModernXP. theme/README.md lists the source and the license of every file of the theme.

When the files of Windows XP are installed in the XDG data directory, as get-microsoft-files.sh of kde-plasma-winxp-launcher does, chora-xp uses them instead of the free files of the theme:

  • fonts/WindowsXP/: XP's Tahoma for the text, Trebuchet MS Bold for the titles and Franklin Gothic Medium Italic for the start button. These fonts go before the system fonts, so XP's Tahoma wins over the Tahoma of newer Windows.
  • wallpapers/WindowsXP/*.jpg: Bliss (bliss.jpg) is the wallpaper instead of Bløff, and Control Panel > Desktop lists all of them.
  • winxp-kde/start_flag.png: XP's flag on the start button, at its own size of 20 pixels.
  • sounds/WindowsXP/stereo/: XP's sounds. login.wav plays when chora-xp starts, logout.wav on Log Off, shutdown.wav on Turn Off and notify.wav when a balloon opens. The first of pw-play, paplay and canberra-gtk-play on the PATH plays them in the background.

chora-xp draws everything as image nodes. It rasterizes the SVG files of the theme with resvg into PNG files in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/chora-xp/. It renders each picture once, at the largest scale of the outputs, but at most 4. Thus text and icons stay sharp on a scaled output. After a change of the scale, it renders the pictures again. The borders of windows and dialogs and the background of the taskbar stay at scale 1. The core reads the insets of a slice in pixels of the file. The pictures:

  • a frame around each window, with its title and the minimize, maximize and close buttons; a window that draws its own frame, as GTK programs do, gets none;
  • a taskbar at the bottom of the work area of each output, with the start button, one button per window of the current desktop, four desktop buttons and a clock;
  • the start menu with the user name, programs, places, the Control Panel, Log Off and Turn Off Computer, and All Programs with the applications of the desktop files in $XDG_DATA_HOME/applications and $XDG_DATA_DIRS, in program groups by their main category;
  • the icons of the desktop, between the wallpaper and the windows;
  • the wallpaper below everything: Bliss when it is installed, else Bløff.

A click on a window raises and focuses it. A drag of a title bar moves the window, and a double click maximizes it. chora-xp claims the box around the work areas of its outputs (D55). --output NAME limits it to some outputs. A window dragged out of these work areas goes to the window manager tiling with remove and to. Without tiling, the window stays. A drag of the border of the frame resizes the window: the 4 pixel border and 6 pixels of the shadow outside it take the press, and the corners reach 16 pixels along both edges. The client gets the new size once per frame while the button is down, and the edges that the drag does not move stay in place. A window is at least 112 by 35 pixels with its frame, so that the buttons of the title bar fit. A window that draws its own frame resizes from a strip of 6 pixels around it. A maximized window does not resize, and a window does not wobble while it resizes. The pointer keeps its arrow over the border: plugins cannot set the cursor. The core reports no size limits of a client yet, so a client that wants another size than it gets simply takes its own, and the frame follows it.

A right click on a title bar, a click on the icon of a title bar and a right click on a task button open XP's system menu, in the look of the context menus below: Restore, Move, Size, Minimize, Maximize and Close in bold with Alt+F4, with XP's glyphs. Restore is gray unless the window is maximized or minimized, Minimize is gray for a minimized window and Maximize for a maximized one. Move and Size are always gray: chora-xp moves and sizes windows with the mouse, and does not have XP's keyboard commands for them. The click on the icon opens the menu below the icon, the others at the pointer. A double click on the icon closes the window, as on XP. A maximized window fills the work area above the taskbar. When an output changes, for example its mode or its scale, its shown windows move back into its work area. A window that does not fit shrinks to it. A click on a task button shows or minimizes its window. Buttons light up under the pointer, and so do the entries of the start menu. All Programs and its groups open their cascading menus when the pointer rests on them for 350 ms, or on a click. A click on a program starts it and closes the menu; a click outside closes the menu. The open menu takes the keyboard. Up and Down move in a column or a cascade. Left and Right go between the columns and into and out of the cascades. Return starts the entry. Escape closes the innermost cascade, then the menu.

The desktop of the first output shows XP's icons in its grid of 75 by 75 pixels: My Documents (XDG_DOCUMENTS_DIR, else the home directory) and My Computer at the top left, then the folders and files of the Desktop folder (XDG_DESKTOP_DIR, else ~/Desktop) by name, folders first, in columns from the top. The Recycle Bin sits at the bottom right and shows whether $XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash/files has files. A desktop file shows its name and icon. A program, a desktop file or a window without an icon gets XP's icon of a program, application-x-executable of the icon theme. Each label is Tahoma in white with a black shadow, in at most two lines. chora-xp looks at the Desktop folder and the trash once a second. The icons that stay keep their cells. A new icon takes the first free cell of the columns. My Network Places is left out, because without a network browser it opens nothing.

A click selects an icon: its label turns white on dark blue, with a dotted focus rectangle while no window has the focus. A click on the empty desktop takes the selection away. A double click opens the icon: a folder, My Documents, My Computer and the Recycle Bin in XP's Explorer (see below); a desktop file runs its program; any other file opens with xdg-open. A drag moves an icon to the nearest free cell of the grid, until chora-xp ends. A drag on the empty desktop draws XP's selection rectangle, in XP's selection blue with a translucent fill and a line of 1 pixel, and selects every icon whose picture or first line of its label it touches, while it grows and shrinks. A drag of one of the selected icons moves all of them, each to the cell at the same offset; if one of them would land on an icon that stays, or two in one cell, they all go back. A click on one of the selected icons selects it alone, and a click on the empty desktop selects nothing. XP has one desktop, so the icons stay in place while the cube turns: each face of the cube shows them on the wallpaper.

The right button opens XP's context menus: white, with a gray border, a soft shadow and the selection in XP's blue. A click on a row does what it says and closes the menu; a click outside closes it. An open menu takes the keyboard. Up and Down move the highlight over the enabled rows. Right opens a submenu, Left closes it. Return does what the row says. Escape closes the submenu, then the menu. Home and End go to the first and the last row. Once a key works the menu, it underlines XP's access keys. A letter acts on the row of its access key, or goes to the next one of several. A drop-down list opens on its current value. While no window has the focus, the desktop takes the keyboard: Shift+F10 and the Menu key open the menu of the selected icon, or of the desktop.

  • The taskbar: Cascade Windows and Tile Windows Horizontally (one above the other) or Vertically (side by side) arrange the windows of the current desktop on the output of the menu; Show the Desktop minimizes them. Lock the Taskbar shows a check mark and changes nothing else, because chora-xp neither moves nor sizes the taskbar. Toolbars and Task Manager are gray: chora-xp has neither.
  • The clock: Adjust Date/Time, then the rows of the taskbar. Customize Notifications is gray.
  • The desktop: Arrange Icons By Name or Type puts the icons back into their columns, in that order; Refresh shows them again; Properties opens Display Properties (see below). Paste and Paste Shortcut are gray.
  • An icon of the desktop: the right button selects the icon and opens XP's menu of its kind. When the icon is part of the selection, the selection stays. The rows act on the icon under the pointer. Open, in bold, does what a double click does. A folder and My Documents have Explore, which opens the folder in Explorer, as My Computer and the Recycle Bin do. Delete of a file or a folder of the Desktop folder asks in XP's Confirm File Delete or Confirm Folder Delete, and Yes moves it to the trash of the freedesktop.org specification: $XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash/files, with its .trashinfo file in Trash/info that holds its percent-encoded path and the date. A name that the trash holds already gets a number, as notes.2.txt. A file on another file system than the trash stays where it is, and chora-xp logs why. Properties shows the type, the folder, the size or the number of items in a folder, and the times it was created, changed and opened. The Recycle Bin has Empty Recycle Bin while it holds files, and its Properties count them. Send To, Open With, Search, Cut, Copy, Create Shortcut and Rename are gray, as are Delete of My Documents and all rows of My Computer but Open and Explore: its Properties would be XP's System Properties.
  • A program or a place of the start menu, or a program of All Programs: Open in bold, Explore for the folders, Remove from This List for the programs of the left column, which leave the menu until chora-xp ends, and Properties with the name, the icon and the command or the folder. Run as, Pin to Start menu, Send To and Rename are gray.

chora-xp draws XP's Windows Explorer itself, as the client of a window of its own: the window has XP's frame and a task button with the icon and the name of the place, and it raises on a click, minimizes through the magic lamp, maximizes and wobbles like the windows of clients. It opens at 785 by 559 pixels, the size of XP's My Computer, or smaller on a small output, and resizes from its edges down to 428 by 294 pixels: the task pane keeps its width, and the view and its scroll bar take the rest. From the top:

  • the menu bar with File, Edit, View, Favorites, Tools and Help, and XP's flag when it is installed. A click opens a menu: File > Close closes the window; View has Tiles, Go To (Back, Forward, Up One Level, My Documents, My Computer, Recycle Bin) and Refresh. The other rows are gray;
  • the Standard Buttons: Back, Forward and Up, as the history of the window allows, and Views with Tiles. Search and Folders are gray. Up goes from My Computer and the Recycle Bin to the Desktop folder, where they sit on XP;
  • the address bar with the path and the icon of the place, its list of places, and Go, which shows the place again;
  • the blue task pane with XP's boxes: the tasks of the place, Other Places and Details. A click on the title of a box closes or opens it. The links of Other Places go to the parent folder, My Documents and My Computer, and Shared Documents when it exists, in the same window; Control Panel and Change a setting open the Control Panel of the start menu. The tasks that change files and My Network Places are gray.

The view of a folder is XP's Tiles view: a 48 pixel icon for each folder and file, its name, and in gray its type and size as XP writes them, such as Text Document and 12.3 KB. Folders come first, then the files by name without case and with numbers by their value (file2 before file10); hidden files, whose name starts with a dot, are left out. The icon comes from the extension: folder, text, image, audio, video, archive, program (also a file that may run) or other. A click selects an item, and Details shows its type, date and size; a click on the empty view selects nothing. A double click opens a folder in the same window, with Back, Forward and Up, and a file with xdg-open. A view longer than the window gets XP's blue scroll bar: its arrows scroll by 40 pixels, a click on the track by a page, and the thumb follows a drag. A notch of the mouse wheel scrolls by 120 pixels, three lines as on XP. A touchpad scrolls as far as the fingers move.

My Computer shows XP's groups under their headings with the blue line: Files Stored on This Computer with Shared Documents (XDG_PUBLICSHARE_DIR, when it exists) and "USER's Documents" (My Documents); Hard Disk Drives; and Devices with Removable Storage. The drives come from /proc/self/mounts: the mounts of disk file systems (btrfs, ext2 to ext4, xfs, f2fs, vfat, exfat, NTFS and others) and of discs, each device once at its shortest mount point, without the bind mounts of a container below /dev, /sys, /proc, /etc, /var/lib and /var/log. A disk is "Local Disk (/)"; a medium below /run/media or /media, or a disc, is removable and goes by the name of its directory. Details shows the file system, the free space and the size, from df. A double click opens a drive or a folder in the same window.

The Recycle Bin lists the trash of the freedesktop.org specification, $XDG_DATA_HOME/Trash/files, with the folder each item came from and the date it went, from its file in Trash/info. Recycle Bin Tasks has Empty the Recycle Bin, gray while the bin is empty. It asks first, in XP's Confirm File Delete or Confirm Multiple File Delete, and Yes deletes the files and folders of the trash and their info files for good. Restore all items is gray. Each question of chora-xp takes the keyboard while it shows, and Escape answers No.

My Documents, My Pictures and My Music of the start menu (XDG_DOCUMENTS_DIR, XDG_PICTURES_DIR and XDG_MUSIC_DIR, else the home directory and its folders Pictures and Music) and My Computer open in Explorer too, and the window calls these folders by their names in XP.

Desktop icons dropped on the window of a folder go into the folder, or into the folder item under the pointer. On a file item, or on another window such as a program or My Computer, they go back to their places, as XP does not allow that drop. A file or a folder moves on the same file system and is copied to another one, as XP moves on one drive and copies to another. When the folder has a file of the name, XP's Confirm File Replace asks first, for each such file in turn. Yes replaces the file. A folder on either side of a name stays, and chora-xp logs it. A drop on the window of the Recycle Bin, or on its desktop icon, asks first, as Delete does. Yes sends the files to the Recycle Bin. Beyond this and Empty the Recycle Bin, the window changes no file. The keyboard does not work it (D45). Its icons come from the icon theme, XP's own when WindowsXP of get-microsoft-files.sh is installed.

The Control Panel opens as a menu, as with XP's "Display as a menu". A check mark shows the current choice of each entry, and a click on an entry applies it and closes the menu:

  • Date and Time: opens Date and Time Properties;
  • Desktop: the wallpaper of every output, from the PNG, JPEG and SVG files in wallpapers/WindowsXP of the XDG data directories, theme/wallpaper/ and /usr/share/backgrounds, without their subdirectories and at most 20 of each directory;
  • Display: opens Display Properties;
  • Effects: wobbly windows, the magic lamp, the desktop cube and XP's sounds, on or off until chora-xp ends;
  • Taskbar and Start Menu: opens Taskbar and Start Menu Properties.

Properties of the taskbar menu, and Control Panel > Taskbar and Start Menu, open XP's Taskbar and Start Menu Properties. chora-xp draws this dialog itself, in XP's Luna style: the frame of the theme with the title and the close button, tabs, group boxes, check boxes, radio buttons and push buttons that light up under the pointer. A drag of the title bar moves it, and it wobbles as a window does, as do Date and Time, Display Properties and the other dialogs that XP lets move; the Log Off and Turn Off dialogs stay fixed in the middle. The close button and Cancel close it without a change, OK takes the changes and closes it, and Apply takes them and keeps it open. The dialog stays above the windows, and the keyboard does not work it (D45). The settings last until chora-xp ends:

  • Taskbar shows a preview of the taskbar above its check boxes. Lock the taskbar only changes the check mark, as in the context menu. Auto-hide the taskbar lets the taskbars slide away half a second after the pointer left them, down to a strip of 2 pixels at the bottom edge; the pointer on the strip brings a taskbar back. The work area then reaches down to the strip, and maximized windows grow into it. Keep the taskbar on top of other windows puts the taskbars above the windows, or below them when it is off. Show the clock shows the clock in the notification area, or shrinks the area without it. Group similar taskbar buttons, Show Quick Launch, Hide inactive icons and Customize are gray: chora-xp has neither grouping, Quick Launch nor hidden icons.
  • Start Menu shows a preview of the start menu. The Classic Start menu and the Customize buttons are gray: chora-xp has only XP's start menu.

A double click on the clock, Adjust Date/Time of the clock menu and Control Panel > Date and Time open XP's Date and Time Properties, drawn in the same way:

  • Date & Time shows the month in a drop-down list and the year with arrow buttons, the month calendar with weeks from Sunday and the chosen day in blue, the analog clock with its moving hands and the digital time. A click on the list opens the twelve months, the arrows change the year and a click on a day chooses it. Below, it names the time zone of the system: TZ, else the link /etc/localtime.
  • Time Zone shows the zone with its offset from GMT. XP's world map is left out.

chora cannot set the clock of the system without privileges, so the dialog changes nothing: OK, Cancel and the close button close it, and Apply stays gray. Internet Time is left out.

Properties of the desktop menu and Control Panel > Display open XP's Display Properties, 404 by 455 pixels, drawn in the same way. It opens on the tab that was open when it last closed, Themes the first time. Apply and OK show the background on every output and set the scale of the output of the dialog; Cancel and the close button close it without them. The settings last until chora-xp ends:

  • Themes shows the sample of the theme: the wallpaper with an active window and the Recycle Bin. Windows XP is the only theme, so the list, Save As and Delete are gray.
  • Desktop shows XP's monitor with the chosen background, and the list Background: (None) and the wallpapers of Control Panel > Desktop, with arrows and a track that scroll it. A click on a row chooses it. Position places the picture: Center at its own size in the middle, Tile repeated from the top-left corner, Stretch over the screen out of its aspect ratio, and Fill, which XP lacks, over the screen at its aspect ratio with the overflow cut off, as Windows 7 names it. Fill is the default, so that Bliss keeps its shape on a wide output; XP's own default is Stretch. Color chooses the color of the desktop behind a centered picture, or without one, from a palette of twelve colors with XP's desktop blue first. Browse is gray: chora-xp has no file chooser yet. Customize Desktop is gray too.
  • Screen Saver shows the monitor and XP's controls, all gray: chora-xp has no screen saver and no power settings.
  • Appearance shows a sample with an inactive window, an active window and a message box on the color of the desktop. The style, the color scheme and the font size are gray, as is Advanced. Effects opens a small dialog with check boxes for the wobbly windows, the magic lamp, the desktop cube and the sounds, as Control Panel > Effects; OK takes them.
  • Settings shows the monitor with the desktop and a taskbar, and the name of the output. The slider of Screen resolution chooses the scale of the output, 200 %, 150 %, 125 % or 100 % from Less to More, and names the size that it gives, such as "1280 by 800 pixels". Color quality, Troubleshoot and Advanced are gray.

Log Off and Turn Off Computer open XP's dialogs in the middle of the output, and the desktop behind them fades to gray in 1.5 seconds. In Log Off Windows, Log Off asks every window to close. Switch User is always disabled, because chora has no second session to switch to. In Turn off computer, Stand By runs systemctl suspend. Without systemctl, Stand By is disabled. Turn Off ends chora-xp and shuts nothing down. Restart runs chora-xp again in the same process, with the same arguments. The core keeps the nodes of chora-xp for the grace time of resume (see API). The windows keep their places, desktops, maximized state and stacking. The Explorer windows open again. The current desktop stays, and its top window gets the focus. Cancel or a click outside the dialog closes it. The buttons light up under the pointer; the keyboard does not work the dialogs, for the same reason as Escape.

chora-xp serves notifications (org.freedesktop.Notifications on the session bus), so that notify-send and programs show XP's balloon tips: a pale yellow balloon with a black border above the notification area of the first output, with a tail towards the tray, the icon of the notification, a bold title, the text wrapped at 300 pixels and a close button. While a balloon shows, the notification area grows for its icon, or XP's information icon, left of the clock, as on XP, and the tail points at it. One balloon shows at a time, and the others wait their turn. A balloon closes after its time, which is 10 seconds by default and, as on XP, at least 10 and at most 30 seconds; with a time of 0 it stays until a click. A click on the close button dismisses it; a click on the balloon invokes the action default of the notification, if it has one, and dismisses it too. If another server, such as GNOME Shell, owns the name on the bus, chora-xp logs one line and shows no balloons; it never takes the name from its owner.

The effects run in the plugin, which computes their meshes and transforms at 60 Hz:

  • Wobbly windows. A dragged window bends like jelly: the point under the pointer follows it, the far side lags behind, and after the release the window shakes until it settles.
  • Magic lamp. Minimize pours the window into its task button, and a click on the button pours it out again.
  • Desktop cube. Four desktops sit on the faces of a cube. A turn shows the cube in perspective, and the windows fly off their faces and land again. The taskbar lists the windows of the current desktop.

If frames get too slow because of chora-xp, the core drops its effects; chora-xp then goes without them for 15 seconds. A drop of the effects of another client changes nothing.

Binding Action Alt+F4 close the focused window Ctrl+Escape open or close the start menu Alt+Space open the system menu of the focused window; chora-xp takes the key only while one of its windows has the focus Alt+Tab, Alt+Shift+Tab open XP's switcher with the windows of the desktop, the most recent first. Tab chooses the next window, Shift+Tab the previous window. The release of Alt activates the chosen window. Minimized windows come last. Escape closes the switcher without a switch. Super+e start the terminal Ctrl+Alt+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Right turn the cube to the previous or next desktop Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Left, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Right turn the cube and take the focused window along Super and a drag with the left button turn the cube with the pointer. A drag over the width of the output is a quarter turn. At the release, the cube turns to the nearest desktop. a desktop button 1 to 4 turn the cube to that desktop

The safety layer keeps only Ctrl+Alt with BackSpace, Escape, i and F1 to F12, so the cube takes Ctrl+Alt with the arrows. Ctrl+Alt+i is the revoke binding of Safety layer. When another client holds these bindings, Super+Ctrl with the arrows stands in.

chora-xp exports methods for other clients (see Plugin methods). Each one answers with nothing.

Method Parameters Does the same as start_menu open: whether the menu should be open afterwards a click on the start button of the first output minimize surface a click on the task button of the active window restore, activate surface a click on the task button: the window comes back, is raised and focused, and the cube turns to its desktop restart none Restart in the Turn Off dialog turn_to desktop: a number from 0 to 3 a click on the desktop button Option Default Meaning --theme DIR /usr/share/chora/flavors/xp/theme, or CHORA_XP_THEME the theme directory --terminal CMD foot the terminal of the start menu and of Super+e; CMD -e runs the programs with Terminal=true --launcher CMD fuzzel Run in the start menu, and All Programs when no desktop file lists a program --program TITLE=CMD another program in the start menu; repeat for more --clock FORMAT %-I:%M %p the clock, in the format of strftime --wallpaper FILE Bliss if installed, else Bløff a PNG, JPEG or SVG file --slow-motion FACTOR 1 stretch the magic lamp and the cube, to show them slowly --no-sounds start without XP's sounds; Control Panel > Effects > Sounds turns them on

To try the flavor from a source tree, start it nested:

cargo build --workspace
PATH=$PWD/target/debug:$PATH chora -- chora-xp --theme flavors/xp/theme

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service runs as a Quadlet unit with Podman, or in distrobox. It connects to the IPC socket, appears as a Wayland client, or both. A container mounts only its client directory, which choractl clients create NAME makes (in Quadlet: %t/chora/clients/NAME). It sets CHORA_SOCKET to the ipc.sock and WAYLAND_DISPLAY to the wayland.sock in that directory. The directory of the core holds the admin socket, so a container never mounts it (see API). Through its ipc.sock, the container sees and changes only its own nodes and the windows of its wayland.sock. It sets no camera and puts no node under screen:*. It takes the keyboard with focus_node or focus only after a press of the user on it.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The decision log. It lists the decisions that hold. Every entry can come back for review. The Roadmap names the milestone of a decision that the code does not implement yet.

docs.title: Principles and scope
docs.text: # Decision Reason D1 Rust and Smithay for the core Smithay is a library without policy, proven in niri and cosmic-comp. Rust is safe when agents change the system live. D2 Everything is a plugin Maximum flexibility and a small core. D3 chora 1.0 is a daily driver with a stable, versioned API; until then, the API changes without notice A stable API needs real use first. No compatibility code before 1.0. D4 Reuse before writing; check alternatives for every decision Little code to maintain. D5 One vocabulary, defined in the Glossary One language for people and agents. D6 Inventory and agent memory form a separate layer, not part of the core The platform stays neutral. D7 The name is chora, always in lowercase See Vision. D8 The core is GPL-3.0-or-later; code under GPL-3.0-only stays out The core can then reuse code from Pinnacle and niri. D9 English for code and documentation The documentation is public.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: # Decision Reason D10 Fedora 44 and secureblue as host; a derived image offers chora as an additional session The system and the image tooling of the author. D11 The reference hardware is the HP ZBook Ultra G1a (AMD Radeon 8060S); CI adds a VM with vkms; Intel works through Mesa without a gate; NVIDIA comes later Gates need one machine that the author uses every day. The VM covers the tty backend in CI. D12 Services run as Quadlet units with Podman or in distrobox Isolation. systemd handles start, restart and order. D13 The coordinator is the user first, later an agent with special permissions A gradual path to control by agents. D14 Releases build an RPM only, attached with its SHA256 sum to a GitHub release; versions below 1.0 and release candidates are pre-releases One build for the release assets and the package repository of D49.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D15 Build on Smithay; copy from Pinnacle, niri and anvil; no fork A fork of Pinnacle keeps less than half of its code. See Alternatives. D16 Pin a Smithay git revision No Smithay release since 0.7.0. All major users track git. D17 A scene renderer of chora on GLES 3, on the GL context of Smithay's GlesRenderer; GLSL shaders Smithay's render elements are axis-aligned rectangles. A renderer of its own draws the full 4x4 model and keeps textures between frames. wgpu has no usable dmabuf path for a compositor. D18 Six node kinds: group, surface, rect, image, shader and text Widgets come from Wayland clients. An image node shows a PNG asset, for example a window border, without a client per window. A shader can read another node as a texture. A text node lets plugins and agents label a HUD without a client or a rendered PNG. cosmic-text does the shaping and the font fallback, so the node stays small: text, font family, size, color and maximum width; no editing and no rich text. D19 Transforms are 4x4 matrices; the scene is 2.5D: planes in perspective, meshes and fragment shaders, without a depth test 3D effects need no API change. Complex 3D scenes belong in clients (see Idea backlog). D20 One logical scene; each output shows it through a camera Pan, zoom and the infinite canvas need no extra mechanism. D21 The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces; toplevels wait for a plugin The protocols define these positions. Smithay implements them. D22 A transaction completes when all affected clients commit, or after a deadline; transactions on disjoint surfaces do not wait for each other A resize needs a client round trip. One slow client must not stop the others. D23 A hardcoded safety layer: Ctrl+Alt+Backspace quits, Ctrl+Alt+Escape resets, Ctrl+Alt+F1 to F12 switch the VT, SIGUSR1 resets while the main loop runs; a watchdog that blames the client whose visible nodes cost the most for slow frames, removes its effects and then disconnects it, and never resets the session (target: the watchdog in its own thread; it runs on the main loop, so a hung shader stops it too); a binding that revokes the capabilities of all clients A recovery path must not depend on a file that an agent can break, or on a main loop that hangs. One client without grants must not take the window manager, the grants and the effects of the others down with it. D24 The core renders an output only when it has damage; a layer keeps its texture until its subtree changes; a fullscreen surface without effects uses direct scanout Battery life and GPU load. D25 No undo history and no plugin state store in the core A destroyed client cannot come back. The reset and the views in git cover recovery. The scene holds all state. D26 Xwayland through xwayland-satellite Keeps the core small. D27 Output configuration through wlr-output-management and through output.configure, on the same path kanshi and wlr-randr exist. An agent has no wlr-randr in every session.

docs.title: Plugins and API
docs.text: # Decision Reason D28 Plugins are IPC clients; the core offers animate and frame events with the predicted presentation time; in-process WASM plugins come only after a measurement shows the need Agents work in seconds, not frames. One mechanism, any language, crash isolation by the OS. tests/ipc-bench.sh measures a transaction with a mesh of 8x8 cells at 0.17 ms in the median and 3.6 ms at the 99th percentile, nested and with software rendering. D29 JSON-RPC 2.0 with one message per line on Unix sockets; hello negotiates the protocol version and the features; errors carry a stable code and data Agents and shell scripts reach it without bindings. A versioned protocol lets plugins in other repositories check what they get. D30 The core starts one startup command with WAYLAND_DISPLAY and CHORA_SOCKET set The startup command starts the plugins, or a systemd target. D31 The owner of a node is a client name; only the owner changes a node; another client requests a change, and the core sends the request to the owner; plugins export methods with a description and a JSON schema An agent asks the window manager instead of fighting it. D32 Queries use JSON filters; a query returns all current matches; subscriptions start with a snapshot, and events have sequence numbers A schema describes the filters. Agents get predictable results and miss no event. D33 Each client has a socket directory with an IPC socket and a Wayland socket of its own that hides the privileged protocols; the socket fixes its name and its capabilities; input.inject, screen.capture, input.grab-any, methods.call and activation.token are capabilities A client cannot take another name or give itself capabilities. A container mounts one directory and needs no configuration. D34 MCP outside the core: choractl mcp over stdio on rmcp, with tools for whole tasks and one tool per exported plugin method The core stays free of MCP. The official SDK carries the protocol. D35 The core reads no configuration; choractl loads YAML views and ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml; a flavor is a directory with a systemd target; the configuration holds no secrets Policy and service management do not belong in the core. D36 The GitHub organization is chora-desktop (chora is taken). It holds chora (the core, chora-scene, choractl, the reference documentation), the plugins in repositories of their own, chora-website, chora-packaging, chora-voice and .github. The organization and this split come after 1.0; until the split, the core repository holds the core, the plugins and the services, and they build with it Plugins and services get their own owners and releases once the API of chora-scene is frozen at 1.0. The core keeps the definition of the API. D58 A client changes how a node of another client looks, its opacity, effects or meta, only through the owner: node.requested has the action update (D31). The window manager applies the change and keeps it across layouts The owner stays the only client that changes its nodes. A look that a new layout drops does not hold. D59 The answer of scene.apply carries warnings with stable codes, for example for a surface attached under a group with input: pass, or for a layer that alone is larger than the pixel budget of every output; a drop at render time stays the event layers.dropped Some transactions succeed but do not give the result that the client expects. A warning tells the client without a capture. D61 choractl mcp keeps keep_nodes; after a restart, an agent removes its own old nodes (#101) No change in the core or in choractl. An agent knows which of its nodes still matter.

docs.title: Tools around the core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D37 Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr No code. A portal backend of its own is in the Idea backlog. D38 HTML content from agents runs in a browser in app mode, as a service No code. chora places toplevels anywhere. D39 The XP showroom is a flavor in the style of Windows XP with wobbly windows, a magic lamp minimize and a 3D desktop cube; it lives in the core repository (D36); it is a demo on top of the generic plugins, not a daily driver; it starts installed programs, draws no programs into the scene, and draws its own wallpaper, one per cube face; after its rework in 0.8, it gets fixes and the API ports of the core only, and no release per milestone It proves that the scene model carries classic desktops and their effects, and it tests every API change. The assets come from kde-plasma-winxp-launcher and keep their licenses; the GPL-3.0-only artwork of Exposé and modernXP is data of the flavor, not code of the core (D8). D40 The user gives capabilities in ~/.config/chora/clients.yaml; choractl clients up creates the client sockets through an admin socket that only choractl uses; the emergency reset removes all client sockets; choractl mcp has no tool for capabilities The core draws no text, so a dialog is no option. Only the user changes the capabilities. D41 choractl reads YAML with serde-saphyr: strict booleans, errors on unknown and duplicate keys and on unknown tags serde_yaml is archived and serde_yml is unsound. serde-saphyr is maintained, pure Rust and panic-free, and limits the work of a document. D42 The core starts no program except the startup command. choractl run starts programs through systemd-run --user with an activation token, and journald keeps their output. Without a running user manager, choractl run starts the program as its own child. systemd units restart plugins, and choractl restart restarts such a unit. systemd already supervises processes. Test sessions and sandboxes have no user manager; the fallback lives in choractl, so the core stays free of forks and one binary serves both. The activation token links a program to its window. D43 Nodes fixed to the screen live under one overlay root per output, screen:NAME: in the logical coordinates of the output, without its camera, above the scene and below the top and overlay layers of layer shell A HUD stays in place while a camera moves. A root per output answers on which output a node shows. Its nodes work as all others: input, effects, ownership. D44 output.configure sets scale and transform of an output through the API, on the same path as wlr-output-management One path keeps both ways in step. D45 Grabs need Ctrl, Alt or Super, except for a client with the capability input.grab-any; input.ungrab ends a grab; a key grab tells when the first of its modifiers goes up, except Shift; there is no exclusive keyboard grab Typing works unless the user gives a capability, for example for push-to-talk. Games and 3D clients get every key through Wayland.

docs.title: Process
docs.text: # Decision Reason D46 Each milestone has a gate: CI jobs and checks on the reference hardware with a log as evidence, tracked in a gate issue; the next milestone of the core starts when the gate holds Breadth without real use hides faults. A gate makes "done" checkable. D47 The git flow of the project conventions: main holds chore: init and merge commits; work happens on dev, and each contributor of a shared repository has dev-NAME; a release is a merge into main and an annotated tag on the merge commit; the tag starts the release, which needs green CI of the same commit; commitizen writes the changelog; a review loop runs until a round finds nothing that matters; main accepts pull requests only from the move to the organization after 1.0 (D36) One flow in every repository. A release never ships a red commit. D48 The core is a library and a binary; IPC, transactions, focus and grants have unit tests with a fake clock; a headless GLES backend on the software driver of Mesa runs pixel tests in process; each bug fix comes with a test that fails without the fix Pixel tests in a headless sway cannot reach the internals. Review finds faults that tests should catch. D49 Packages through COPR with Packit, with a subpackage per plugin; no AUR packages The image build and updates need a package repository. D50 The session starts through uwsm; a flavor is a systemd target uwsm handles the environment and the graphical session target. D51 The daily driver of milestone 0.9 (D60) is chora-tiling with waybar, fuzzel, mako, swaybg, swaylock, swayidle and kanshi; panel and launcher plugins of chora come after 1.0 Existing tools cover the shell. Own plugins are no condition for 0.9 or 1.0. D52 The milestones run 0.6 to 1.0 as in the Roadmap A stable API needs real use and a testable core first. D53 The voice pipeline lives in chora-voice, until the split after 1.0 in services/voice/ of the core repository (D36), and runs in parallel to the core; the core supplies push-to-talk grabs, text injection, the read model and an agent indicator The pipeline is a product of its own. It needs only the API of the core. D54 Plugins use the JSON-RPC API with frame events and fd passing; a private Wayland protocol for plugins comes only if a measurement at 120 Hz in milestone 0.10 shows the need One API to maintain. The measurement decides. D55 Window managers share the scene through claims. A claim is a scene area of one window manager. A window manager hands a surface to another with remove and to. The core gives a new toplevel to a window manager (see below). The user chose one window manager per claim over a single window manager role. Ownership, attach and surface.detached stay the mechanism, and a camera switches between claims. D56 The UI is hybrid. Plugins draw shell chrome and effects as scene nodes. Real applications, such as a file manager or a control panel, run as Wayland clients. Scene nodes take the keyboard through focus_node. In 0.8, chora-xp stops drawing programs into the scene and starts installed programs instead (D39). The git tag archive/xp-scene-programs keeps the removed code Chrome and effects need the scene: transforms, shaders, wobble. Applications need text input, accessibility and toolkits, which clients bring. D57 The watchdog disconnects a client for slow frames only when its own visible load reaches the owner budget, CHORA_OWNER_LOAD_BUDGET with a default of 4000. Below it the slowdown is shared: the watchdog removes the effects of all clients and disconnects none The W5 battle disconnected a playing snake while a budget probe churned its nodes. The largest single load was not the fault. Two clients that are each half the fault should keep their connections, and the frame still gets cheap; a client alone over its budget is the clear culprit. D60 The daily driver comes before the renderer: milestone 0.9 is the daily driver and 0.10 the renderer Daily use needs a stable session more than a faster renderer. 0.9 takes from the renderer only the watchdog thread, which detects a hung main loop.

docs.title: D55: window managers per claim
docs.text: Issue #73 calls the area of a window manager a view. The glossary uses "view" for a YAML arrangement (D5), so this design says claim. The design has two steps. Step 1 is the handover. Step 2 adds claims and the routing of new toplevels.

docs.title: Step 1: handover
docs.text:
Window manager A hands surface s1 to window manager B:

  1. A owns s1, for example at the end of a drag out of its area. A knows B by a fixed name or by a meta tag on the root group of B.
  2. A sends remove: {id: s1, to: B}. to must name a connected client. As at every remove, the surface becomes detached and loses the keyboard focus.
  3. The core reserves s1 for B and sends surface.detached, which carries the surface alone. An attach of another client fails.
  4. B attaches s1, places it by its own rules, and can give it the focus. A plugin that adopts every detached surface needs no change.
  5. When the last connection of B closes, the reservation ends. With resume, it ends after the grace time. The core then sends surface.detached to all, and any client can attach the surface.

Focus and grabs. The keyboard focus does not move with the surface. The receiving window manager sets it with focus after the attach. Grabs belong to connections and do not move. A ends its drag at the release of the button, and then hands the surface over. The client of the surface keeps its pointer and keyboard input as before.

docs.title: Step 2: claims
docs.text:
A claim is a rectangle in scene coordinates: the property claim: [x, y, w, h] of a node. The owner of the node holds the claim. A window manager sets it on its root group, and the claim ends with its node. Window managers claim the whole work area of their outputs. An output shows a claim through its camera. So two window managers sit on two outputs, or at two places in the scene, and a camera move switches one output between them. With claims, A finds B in the claims of scene.query.

At the first commit of a toplevel, the core picks its window manager. The first choice is the owner of its parent toplevel, so that a dialog stays with the manager of its window. The next choice is the owner of the focused node, or of the focused surface, if it holds a claim. The last choice is the owner of the smallest claim that contains the pointer. A client that asked for an activation token (D42) does not win by the token itself. The core reserves the surface for that client, as at a handover. Outside of all claims, any window manager can take the new surface.

Out of scope for now.

  • The drop position: B places the surface by its own rules.
  • A drag that continues in B after the handover.
  • An embedded GNOME session in a claim.
  • Claims under screen:NAME.

docs.text: Proposal Reason Versioned docs with mike are too much The project conventions use mike. Hooks without matching files The project conventions use this hook set in every repository. Cairo and Pango, or another 2D engine, in the core The core composites and draws no vector graphics. Text comes from the text node on cosmic-text (D18), shapes from rects and shader nodes. Plugins draw rich chrome themselves, for example with tiny-skia and resvg. An exclusive keyboard grab Typing must work. Clients that need every key get it through Wayland (D45). A 3D node with depth buffer in the core It makes the core an engine. 3D scenes belong in clients (D19). A rewrite from scratch The scene model, the API and the safety layer hold. The milestones change the rest step by step (D52).

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary of chora. Code, docs and prompts to agents use these terms and no synonyms.

Term Meaning Core The compositor process chora. It handles the Wayland protocols, the backends (DRM/KMS, libinput), the scene, the renderer, the input routing, the IPC socket and the safety layer. It contains no policy. Scene The tree of nodes that the core renders. It is the single source of truth for the screen content. Node One element of the scene. The kinds are group, surface, rect, image, shader and text. Every node has an id, an owner, a transform, an opacity and optional effects. Group A node that contains other nodes. It applies a transform, a clip, an opacity and optional effects to its children. Canvas A group that serves as a working area: a workspace, a desktop or an infinite zoomable plane. Surface A node that shows a Wayland client: an application window, a layer-shell widget or a browser window. For the core, a surface is a texture source and an input target. Rect A colored rectangle with optional rounded corners and border. Shader A node that a fragment shader draws completely. A shader can read other nodes as textures. A shader can also be an effect. Effect A shader that changes how a node and its children look, for example blur or a color change. Every node can have effects. Camera The part of the scene that one output shows: a transform from scene coordinates to the logical coordinates of the output. Claim A scene area of one window manager (D55). Work area The part of the scene that an output shows, without the zones that panels and IPC clients reserve. Plugins place windows in it. Client A process on the IPC socket: a plugin, choractl or a service. A client names itself when it connects. Owner The client name that created or attached a node. Only the owner changes the node. Toplevel A surface with the role of an application window (xdg_toplevel). Other roles are layer surfaces and popups. Detached The state of a surface node without a parent. A detached surface is not visible. View A declarative arrangement: nodes, the plugins that drive them, and their configuration. A view is a YAML file in git. The user or an agent changes it live. Plugin A client that reacts to events, changes the scene and can export methods. A window manager, a layout, an animation set and a keybinding set are plugins. Service A process in a container, outside the core. Examples are speech recognition, a local LLM and a development environment. Flavor A preconfigured bundle of views, plugins and services, for example "classic", "tiling" or "agentic". Coordinator The party that installs and connects plugins, services and flavors. First the user, later an agent with special permissions. Inventory A local, git-versioned store of reusable elements (views, plugins, widgets). It belongs to the opinionated layer above chora, not to the core. Command A request to change the scene, for example create or update. Event A message from the core about a change, for example surface.created. Selector An expression that finds nodes by id, attribute or meta data, for example app_id:firefox. Transaction A batch of commands that the core applies as one unit. If one command fails, the core applies none of them. Capability A right of a client beyond the scene API: input.inject, screen.capture, input.grab-any, methods.call and activation.token. A client socket fixes the capabilities of its name (D33). Grant A capability that a client name holds: from choractl grant on the main socket, or from clients.yaml for a client socket. Milestone A minor release on the way to 1.0, with a goal, a scope and a gate. See Roadmap. Gate The checks that end a milestone; see Roadmap. Safety layer The only built-in behavior of the core: fixed bindings, emergency reset, session lock, watchdog.

• A wake word in addition to push-to-talk for the voice pipeline (D53).
  • A morning view: greeting, current tasks, sorted email, and a day plan that user and agent prioritize together.

It renders with Vulkan, for example with Bevy or Godot, and chora shows its surface as a node, without a copy through dmabuf. The client gets plain keys with press, release and repeat, and relative pointer motion for a mouse look, as every Wayland client does. Through IPC or MCP it moves cameras and panels.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The layout of this repository: one Cargo workspace with as few crates as possible. A module moves into its own crate only when a second consumer can use it. The plugins move into repositories of their own with 1.0 (D36).

chora/
├── crates/
│   ├── chora-scene/   # scene model, commands, events, selectors, IPC types and client; no Smithay
│   ├── chora/         # the compositor: Smithay, backends, renderer, input, safety, IPC
│   ├── chora-kit/     # building blocks for plugins: wobbly windows, magic lamp, XDG dirs, icons, desktop entries
│   └── choractl/      # CLI over the IPC socket; `choractl mcp` is the MCP bridge
├── plugins/
│   ├── chora-tiling/  # reference plugin: the tags, layouts and bindings of awesome
│   └── chora-xp/      # stacking window manager in the style of Windows XP
├── flavors/           # systemd units of the flavors; the theme of the XP flavor
├── examples/          # loader prototype and showcase apps over the API
├── services/voice/    # the voice agent and the quadlets of its models
├── dist/              # RPM build script, Fedora build requirements, session files, Quadlet examples
├── tests/             # end-to-end scripts, headless sessions, input probe
├── deny.toml          # cargo-deny: allowed licenses, advisories
├── ruff.toml          # ruff: the rules for the Python in services/voice/
├── docs/              # this documentation (MkDocs)
├── mkdocs.yml
└── Cargo.toml         # workspace, lints

docs.title: Reasons for this split
docs.text:
• chora-scene has no Smithay dependency. Tests of the data model and the transaction logic need no GPU and no compositor. The core, choractl and plugins share this one definition of the API.
  • chora-kit holds the building blocks that plugins share and that are not part of the API of the core: the IPC and event connection, the self-computed effects and the freedesktop files. Today conn is the part with more than one user; code of one plugin stays in that plugin.
  • Reference plugins are workspace members. They keep the API honest.
  • choractl builds the JSON schemas from the Rust types at run time, in crates/choractl/src/schema.rs. The repository does not contain them. The MCP tools and the test of the documentation examples then see the same contract.

docs.text: The path from the current state to chora 1.0. Version 1.0 is a daily driver with a stable, versioned API (D3).

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Each milestone is a minor release: 0.6, 0.7 and so on.
  • Each milestone has a goal, a scope, an estimate and a gate.
  • A milestone gets a firm estimate when its scope is fixed. The table holds a first guess.
  • The gate is a list of checks. A check is a CI job or a step on the reference hardware with a log as evidence (D46).
  • A milestone is done when every check of its gate holds. The next milestone of the core starts only then.
  • Each milestone has a gate issue on GitHub with the checks as a task list. Each ticked check links to its CI run or log. The release of the milestone closes the issue.
  • Two tracks run in parallel to the core: the XP showroom and the voice pipeline.
  • The showroom track has no milestones of its own (see Track: XP showroom).
  • The voice track has milestones of its own. It never blocks the core.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text:
• The core runs nested and as a login session. It has no long run on real hardware.
  • The scene has six node kinds, 4x4 transforms, cameras, overlay roots, meshes, effects and animations.
  • The API covers scene changes, events, grabs, plugin methods, captures, input injection, grants, programs, assets and output configuration.
  • choractl loads views and serves MCP.
  • chora-tiling and the XP showroom are plugins in this repository.
  • The core is a library and a binary. Unit tests run IPC dispatch, transactions, focus and grants in process, without a backend. The tty backend has no tests. One pixel test renders in process on the headless backend. Pixel tests in a headless sway check the behavior.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
The estimates count the lines of Rust that a milestone adds or changes. They also count the hours of agent work and the hours of hands-on work of the user. The calendar time includes the gate. Agent hours include the tests and the review rounds.

The basis is this repository: about 26,000 lines of Rust in 54 hours of calendar time. A rework of existing code costs more than new code. The table uses about 140 to 200 lines per agent hour for 0.6, 0.7 and 0.10. The milestones 0.9 and 1.0 have hardware work and use about 80 to 125.

The user uses chora as the daily session from milestone 0.9. The gates of 0.9 and 1.0 measure that use, so they set the calendar time.
